## Resolved

### Task 11.242 — resolved 2026-09-13 by the planning session

**Measured first, and the measurement corrected the brief in the direction that matters.** The v15
phone does not crash on a null colour — **it never gets that far.** Its own SQLite refuses the row at
`Tags.color_hex TEXT NOT NULL`, the page rolls back, the cursor never advances, **and the phone
reports the wreck as a fault in itself**, pointing the user at *"whoever manages your project
server"*. **That is worse than the crash the brief inherited from 11.240**: a crash is at least
attributable. This one made a correct server look broken and a working phone blame the wrong person,
silently, forever. **The instruction to build the case rather than inherit it is what found that**,
and it is the third time in a fortnight that instruction has paid.

**Option A, as the planning session leaned, and the reasoning held up.** Major 4. A v15 build is now
told *"This version of TriTrack is too old to sync with the server. Update the app to continue
syncing"* — a refusal a person can act on, replacing a dead end they could not diagnose.

**But the real output is the freeze.** `assertWireShapeCompatibleWithMajor` now fails the app,
package and server suites on any change a device on the current major could not survive — a column
deleted, retyped, losing or gaining `NOT NULL`, joining or leaving the key, a bound tightened, a
table removed. **It would have caught 11.240 on the commit that made it.** And it writes down what
it cannot see — a name reused for a new meaning, and the enum sets `RowValidator` keeps in a
`switch` — which is the difference between a guard and a guard that is trusted for more than it does.

**The finding nobody was looking for is the one worth the entry.** Task 11.219 bumped the major on
2026-09-10, and **for three days the backup pipeline labelled every archive of the beta server
"schema major 2" — in the cleartext sidecar and in the signed comment `restore.sh` trusts.** Nobody
reported it. **The failure was not forgetting the backup scripts; it was that no list existed for a
bump to check against**, so forgetting was the only available outcome.

> **`TriTrack_Technical_Context.md` now carries "What speaks the wire and is not the app" — with the
> grep that produced it, and a sentence saying its own table is a hand-maintained list and therefore
> already wrong.** The durable fix is stated there and is not the table: **`gate_wire.py` reads
> `schemaMajorVersion` from source and needed no change at either bump, while three shell scripts
> that spelled the number went stale.** Reading the constant removes a file from the list
> permanently; updating the file removes it until next time. **In `CLAUDE.md` as a rule.**

**Three decisions taken so they are not re-asked:**

1. **`Tags.color_hex` stays.** Dropping it inside major 4 needs `--refreeze`, and **that flag is the
   *"nobody is on that build yet"* argument wearing a flag** — the exact reasoning this task exists
   because of. A few bytes a row is not worth spending the mechanism built to stop us spending
   majors casually. If a later task wants it gone, it is a major 5 with its own justification, **and
   that price is the point.**
2. **`RowValidator`'s enum sets: trip-wire, not a task**, with the trigger written where it will
   fire — the first task that removes an enum value. **The count is what decides it:** zero
   instances. Same ranking as `/11-233` and `/11-236`, and the answer differs by population rather
   than taste — the freeze was built because a shared column *had already* changed shape.
3. **The Technical Context edits this code task made are owned, not reworded.** A code task editing a
   planning document, declared in its report — **correct, because the bump made both sentences
   false**, and I read them and they are right.

**Two open things it declined to couple, recorded because "not coupled" and "forgotten" look
identical later:** `restore.sh`'s `SCHEMA_MIN=1` mirrors the app's private `_lowestMigratableMajor`
and the server suite cannot import it — **a duplicated constant, the same shape as the three scripts
just fixed, and the only one left.** And the backup drill's three assertions now read the constant
but **the drill itself has not been run** (it needs the full stack and twenty minutes) — release
checklist territory, not a claim.

**For Michael, and it is the intended cost:** any build installed before this commit — **including
the one on his phone** — will refuse to sync until rebuilt. **Server first, then the app.** Nothing
is changed or lost by the refusal; the phone waits.

### Task 11.240 — resolved 2026-09-13 by the planning session

**The animal is a row now, and the schema change was as small as the reading predicted** — one table,
one nullable column, colour moving house. Every existing collar became an animal with the same name
and colour. Server suite green on the beta server's **real v11 → v16 path**, which is the evidence
that matters, since that is the machine that will actually run it.

**Its most valuable output is the thing it did not fix.** `Tags.color_hex` went nullable while
`schemaMajorVersion` stayed at **3** — so a v15 app and a v16 server both announce major 3, the
compatibility check passes, they sync, **and the old client crashes on the null colour.**
`TriTrack_Technical_Context.md` says in as many words that the major version *is* the compatibility
boundary: same major syncs, different major refuses. **The boundary is currently declaring two
builds compatible when they are not.**

> **The codebase already argues this exact point from the other direction.** `pulse_modes.dart`
> explains that every added column was made nullable precisely to avoid *"turning a minor schema
> difference into a device that cannot sync."* **This is the mirror image — a column that was
> non-null becoming nullable — and it strands an old reader just as completely, by crashing instead
> of refusing.** Task **11.242, above the line.**

**The brief for it does not inherit the crash.** 11.240 *stated* it; nothing in the repository
demonstrates it, and after a week in which two of this session's own claims were reasoned from
neighbouring facts and wrong, **the first step is to build the case and report the answer even if
nothing crashes.** Then choose: bump the major so an old client refuses cleanly — **free today,
because Michael's is the only device, and not free after March** — or keep a mirrored colour on the
tag, which buys compatibility with the second source of truth 11.240's own brief forbade. **The
inclination is the bump; the measurement decides.**

**And the third item is the one that outlives either choice.** The defect is not the null column —
**it is that nothing noticed.** A shared table's column losing `NOT NULL` without a major bump is a
class, and the task must either check for it or write down why it cannot be checked. **An
unenforceable rule in a document is what this whole entry is about.**

**Three items handed to 11.241, all correct to have been left.** The collar-to-animal link method and
`findByIndividual` exist with no caller — **left out because the uncalled-method guard refuses a
method nothing calls, which is the guard working**, and 11.241 is the caller. The device tag
library's colour was deliberately kept as a seed for the animal created when a collar is copied into
a project; **a seed is not a second source of truth but looks exactly like one**, so 11.241 writes
the distinction down before somebody "fixes" it. And the export button, now at six save dialogs, gets
zipped there — **with a written escape hatch: if it is more than an afternoon it becomes its own
entry rather than swelling that one.**

**Documents done by this session:** `TriTrack_Technical_Context.md` gained an `Individuals` section
and both new `Tags` columns, with the redeployment rule written beside `individual_id` rather than
left to be inferred from its kind. `WEBSITE_PLAN.md` carries the export change and a warning that
**the guide is now wrong wherever it calls a colour the collar's**. §4.13's H-3 sentence is
**deliberately not edited** and is release-checklist item F4: the sweep now probes thirteen tables,
**that is a measurement nobody has taken**, and correcting a security count from a guess is how the
last four count errors happened.

**For Michael, and it is an ordering rule rather than a task:** **deploy the server before handing
anybody a new app build.** A v16 server is safe for a v16 client and safe to run ahead of any client;
the danger is only an old *app*. He has said no such device exists — **11.242 is what makes that
stop being a thing he has to remember.**

### Task 11.239 — resolved 2026-09-13 by the planning session

**It reproduced on the first run, and the task did exactly what it was told to do with that answer:
re-ranked itself above the line and fixed it in the same pass.** An old backup names a collar by the
id it had before 2026-09-10; the phone holds the same animal under the id the fork gave it; both
were kept. **Two tag rows for one animal in one project — the backup's bearings under one, every
bearing taken since under the other.** Now matched by lineage on the way in.

> **This is the argument for writing "measure first, and a clean negative ends the task" into a
> brief.** The finding arrived as a guess from 10.87, which was right to stop rather than act on
> reasoning. Had the brief said *fix the duplicate-tag bug*, the task would have built a repair
> without ever learning whether the repair was needed — and had the answer been one tag, the honest
> outcome was an entry saying so. **The instruction cost one sentence and bought the difference
> between a fix and a guess.**

**Michael counted on his phone, 2026-09-13: no duplicates.** So the one state this task cannot
repair — a device that **already** holds two rows for one collar — **stays theoretical, and that is a
count rather than an assumption.** **No follow-up task is opened**, with the trigger written down:
if anybody reports a collar appearing twice in one project, the entry below becomes live and Phase
12's merge is pulled forward for it.

**One consequence to carry into beta, because it is a dead end rather than a defect.** A device in
that state is now **refused** when it imports an older backup of that project, with a sentence saying
the two records need merging first. **The refusal is right** — importing more data onto a duplicate
compounds it — **but there is no way out of it in the app today.** For Michael that is fine; **for a
beta crew in the field it is a trap with no exit**, and it belongs on the list of things to know
before handing the app to somebody else's team.

**The decision the task took rather than asked is the right one, and is confirmed here.** The
lineage match runs **only on the untrusted-archive path**. A page pulled from the server keeps the
server's ids, because rewriting them on the phone would leave phone and server disagreeing about
which row a bearing belongs to — **and no server has ever held a collar in two projects, so the case
cannot arrive that way.** A test pins it. **Two paths, two rules, and the reason written beside
both** is precisely what was missing when `TileSources.byId` answered a question it should have
refused.

**And it fixed the comment that started this.** `SchemaMigrator`'s v14 sentence said the fork
*"cannot arise in an archive at all"* — true of the archive alone, false of the archive meeting a
forked device. **The most-repeated shape in this catalogue, corrected rather than inherited.**

**Copy is in `WEBSITE_PLAN.md`**, including a flag that *"Tags matched to a collar this project
already had"* describes a **success**, not a problem — a guide sentence calling it a warning would
be wrong. The one developer-worded string is unreachable today and left alone with its own trigger.

### Task 11.237 — acted on 2026-09-13 by the planning session; **stays Partial until a second device**

**Built as decided.** A non-member's imported project says what it is on the projects list, refuses
every change with one sentence that names the join-code path, and offers the server nothing. **The
property worth more than the feature: a real membership arriving by sync turns the same project live,
with nothing to re-import** — because the standing is derived every read rather than stored. That was
the instruction and it held.

**The correction in the report is mine, and it is the same error twice in a week.** My entry said a
non-member's edits *"reach the server, are refused, and pile up."* **Measured: they never left the
device.** An imported project is never marked linked, sync says *not linked* and offers nothing, and
Publish is owner-only. **I inferred a mechanism from two neighbouring facts** — the
server-is-authority comment and the existence of refused rows — **instead of reading the push path.**
**The silence was worse than I described**, not rows rejected somewhere but changes that were never
offered to anything. **Michael's decision was right either way, which is luck and not method** — and
the rule this breaks is already in `CLAUDE.md` under the 11.181 heading.

**Two things it left, and they are one task, 11.238 (Sonnet, below the line):**

1. **A snapshot holder cannot delete the snapshot.** `Projects` is owner-only with a single
   exemption for a *departed* member, and a snapshot holder was never on the project — so no Leave
   and no Delete, and the copy sits in their list until they join or reinstall. **11.237 was right to
   stop:** that exemption's own text says *"adding a second should be as uncomfortable as this one
   was."* **The brief makes it uncomfortable** — the safety argument must be rewritten in the new
   task's words rather than inherited, and the check is *no open membership row **and** no closed
   one*, which is the half that makes it not a copy-paste.
2. **An adopted project is live but not syncing, and says nothing.** A member importing their own
   project onto a new device can record a week of bearings with nothing leaving the phone. **The
   behaviour stays** — linking because a file claims membership trusts the file further than anything
   else does, and the join path exists — **but the silence does not.** One derived sentence naming
   the step that starts syncing, on the shelf 11.237 already built.

> **"Live and syncing" in the plan's table was my wording and was wrong.** Corrected in place. **This
> is the third silent-failure finding in this sequence and all three have the same shape:** the app
> does the correct thing and does not say it. The thread running through 11.235, 11.237 and 11.238 is
> not a class of bug — **it is a habit of not writing the sentence.**

**One rule moved and is recorded rather than left to be rediscovered as a defect:**
`ProjectMembershipRepository.insert` no longer runs the general write gate after its own authority
check, because that row's audit column cannot say who is acting on a grant. **Recorded in Discovered
Scope with its reasoning** — a moved rule that nobody wrote down is the next task's false finding.

**Copy is in `WEBSITE_PLAN.md`, with one trap named:** the plan's phrase *"Changes here stay on this
device"* **was never shipped**, because Michael chose refusal over local-only edits. **Anything
quoting it is wrong.** The guide has no page about receiving somebody else's project, and this is
the first behaviour that makes one worth considering — **raised for the content lane, not written by

### Task 11.235 — acted on 2026-09-13 by the planning session; **one line from Michael closes it**

**The + button opens, the fix is the right one, and the brief's forbidden shortcut stayed forbidden.**
The repair helper now takes no `Ref` at all, and **a source-reading test refuses one being added
back** — which is better than the fix, because the fix is a state and the test is a rule. A tap that
cannot open the form now says so, asserted. `projectById` carries the same change.

**A test next door already knew.** The `saying which way a copy went` group holds a subscription to
`allProjectsProvider` for the test's lifetime, with a comment saying a bare read *"can be disposed
before the rebuild that write triggers finishes."* **The harness had worked around the defect the app
had, and written down why, and nobody read it as a bug report.** That is worth more attention than
the fix: **a workaround in a test is a defect nobody filed** — when a test needs a comment explaining
why the app cannot be used the obvious way, the comment is the finding.

**My own plan entry made the pre-commit suite red**, which is a first. The 11.235 entry quoted the
phone's stack trace **with line numbers**, and task 11.179's citation ratchet counts those as
citations that will go stale. The task rewrote them to name functions instead, inside the entry it
was already editing. **The guard was right and my writing was wrong** — a stack trace is evidence,
and evidence is quoted for its names, not its line numbers, precisely because the lines move.

**The count was wrong for a worse reason than being wrong.** My brief said 117 `await ref.*` lines
across 17 files; it re-derives as 115 across 15. **The two does not matter. The unit does.** A line
reading `await ref.watch(x.future)` is the *safe* form — I had counted the safe and the dangerous
together and called the total a risk. The real derivation, with a measured threshold (Riverpod
disposes a bare-read auto-dispose provider one microtask after the read returns; one `await` of a
resolved future still runs, two throws, any real gap throws) gives **39 auto-disposing providers, 4
with the dangerous shape, 1 reached bare.** **Third count of mine corrected in a week, and the first
where the number was of the wrong thing** — which `CLAUDE.md` already names from task 11.181 and
which is worse than an arithmetic slip, because recounting does not fix it.

**Four decisions taken, so the next task is not asked to re-open them:**

1. **The Sync Status "Try again" defect becomes task 11.236, below the line.** Same fault, different
   screen, measured by a probe. The record *is* released, so nothing is lost and it syncs next round
   — **that is a reason to rank it lower and not a reason to leave it**, because the button still
   lies in the direction that makes a person press it again. **If Michael reports hitting it, it
   moves up that day.**
2. **The three providers one `await` away — `mayWriteProjectData`, `strandedRecordCount`,
   `serverHttpClient` — are fixed in the same task.** The population is four and named, the fix is
   two lines, two sit on paths used constantly and one is sign-in. **No repository-wide guard**: it
   would fire on eleven providers of which seven work today, and **an instrument that cries wolf
   about working code gets silenced — that is precisely how `clippedTexts` ended up pumping five
   test files.** Revisit at a fifth instance.
3. **The owner-membership repair stays inside the read.** The task's written answer is that it is
   safe now *by the absence of one line*, and that the more honest home is once per launch. **Safe
   by an absence is normally this project's warning shape** — the reason it is acceptable here is
   that the absence is now **enforced by a test that refuses a `Ref` parameter**, which converts a
   fragile state into a rule. **The decision rests on that test; if the test goes, so does the
   decision**, and moving the repair to once-per-launch is the fallback, with tasks 8.4 and 11.1's
   transferred-ownership condition as the thing any move must preserve.
4. **The harness boundary goes into 11.236**: `currentProjectProvider` opens no database when there
   is no active project, and most bare widget tests depend on that silently — breaking it hung one
   file **ten minutes per test**. **Second hang in a week from `testWidgets` pinning a timeout that
   `flutter test --timeout` does not override.** It gets a named test that fails with a sentence.

**Status stays Partial by its own acceptance**, which named Michael's phone. He has reported 11.235
complete and tested; **the one line still needed is whether tapping + on the new build opened the
form** — and if it did not, whether the new sentence appeared at the bottom of the screen, which is

### Task 11.235 — opened 2026-09-13 by the planning session, from Michael's phone

**Not a task report — a defect found during a device look asked for by another task, written up
here because that is where it was found.** Michael tapped **+** on the tag database and nothing
happened. **He cannot create a collar; it is above the line.**

**The planning session guessed, and the guess was wrong.** The reasoning was decent — Add is the only
path with a project picker, Edit and read-only were both fine, and task 11.232 had just changed that
picker — **and one log capture disproved it in two minutes**, naming the function and the line: an
auto-disposing provider `ref.watch`ing after an `await`, inside a helper that **writes** while a
screen is only reading. **The guess was labelled a hypothesis and the measurement went first**,
which is the only reason it cost a sentence instead of a task. That is now a rule.

**The deeper fault is worth the task being Opus rather than a one-line patch.**
`_ensureOwnerMembership` repairs data — it backfills a missing owner row — from inside a provider
whose job is to answer *"what projects exist"*, once per project, in a loop, in a provider that can
be discarded at any moment. **It is idempotent, which is exactly why it looked safe.** Idempotent
means safe to repeat; it does not mean safe to **interrupt**. **The brief forbids the `ref.mounted`
patch**, which would stop the exception and leave the button broken — the loop would abandon its
repair silently, which is what it already does.

**And it failed with no message at all.** A person taps, nothing happens, and they have nothing to
report but *"it doesn't work."* **The brief requires that a tap which cannot open the dialog says
so**, asserted by a test — the project's oldest defect class arriving somewhere new.

**`projectById` has the identical shape** and is the Projects list screen's path; `currentProject`
escapes only because it is marked keep-alive, which is luck. **The wider count is reported, not
acted on** — 117 `await ref.watch`/`read` occurrences across 17 provider files, of which only the
auto-disposing-plus-watch-after-await combination is dangerous. **Rank before guarding**, same as
11.233.

### Task 11.231 — resolved 2026-09-13 by the planning session

**Done, clean, and it asked for nothing** — which is worth saying out loud after a week in which
almost every task produced another. All three of 11.230's Discovered Scope items are fixed and
tested: the Erase tool now keeps what a saved area still needs and **says afterwards what it kept
and which area needed it**; coverage and erase share one rule for *inside*; and `TileSources.byId`
refuses an unknown id instead of quietly answering OpenStreetMap.

**The decision taken without asking Michael held up.** Erase subtracts saved areas rather than
warning about them — chosen because erasing too much costs a download needing a connection he does
not have in the field, while erasing too little costs disk space and is undone offline in two taps.
**Nothing in the task's report argues against it**, and the tool keeps its real use: tiles no area
owns are still erased.

**The naming note is taken, not filed.** `OfflineRegionStore` now carries the set-subtraction
machinery generalised from *"one saved area"* to *"a shape a person drew"* — `eraseInPolygon`, with
`tilesInPolygonNoAreaCovers` / `demTilesInPolygonNoAreaCovers` / `tileAreaIdsCovering` /
`demAreaIdsCovering` beneath it. **Any future task that needs the same arithmetic against the
manifest extends these rather than writing a third version**, and that sentence belongs here so the
third version does not get written.

**The dead-source message is the shape to copy.** An area downloaded with a basemap the app no
longer offers now says so on its row, and **can still be deleted** — because the delete uses the
stored source string rather than the lookup. **A record that names its own obsolescence and stays
actionable** is the opposite of the failure that produced this task, where a lookup that could not
fail made a fixture pass by deleting nothing at all.

**No device check.** 11.231's acceptance is arithmetic — does the subtraction come out right, does a
bad lookup refuse — and the suite proves it. **The task said so rather than asking Michael to look at
something a test already settled**, which is the `Done` means a person has looked rule applied
correctly in the other direction.

### Task 11.232 — acted on 2026-09-12 by the planning session; **stays Partial until Michael looks**

**The freeze did not exist, and the escalation was mine.** I put this above the line because a
report said the app hung when somebody opened a collar's details. **It draws in 86 ms at the size it
was called frozen at.** The ten idle minutes were **11.229's own harness eating its failure
message**: `collectLayoutOverflows` decided what an overflow was by asking whether the error text
contained *"overflowed by"*, and the failing `expect` had a `reason:` that quoted a stripe — so the
harness classified its own `TestFailure` as a rendering overflow, the binding asserted inside its
uncaught-error path, and the test could never finish. **Same dialog, same scale, and the only
difference between failing in a second and hanging for ten minutes was whether the message happened
to quote the stripe.**

**Separating the two failures, because they need different fixes.** Escalating on that evidence was
not a bad judgement — a freeze reachable from a documented OS setting genuinely is not shippable, and
that paragraph stands in the entry. **The evidence was wrong, and the step that was skipped is
identifiable:** *"the CPU was idle"* was written down and never asked what it meant. **A looping
layout burns a core; an idle hang is an unfinished wait.** Those are different diagnoses and the
sentence contained the answer. The entry is re-ranked to below the line on the corrected facts, with
the original argument left standing rather than deleted.

**Three rules already in `CLAUDE.md` would each have caught this, and none was reached for** — the
idle-CPU question, naming a cause from a resemblance without a measurement, and 11.181's *when you
enumerate hypotheses, the measurement is one of the candidates.* **A rule that exists and is not
reached for is not yet a habit**, so the trigger is now written plainly: **a test that hangs, a probe
that times out — suspect the instrument first and prove it innocent before describing the app at
all.** Two mechanical facts went in beside it: `testWidgets` pins a ten-minute timeout that
`flutter test --timeout` does not override (thirty minutes instead of ninety seconds), and **an
instrument that classifies by matching words in a message is guessing** — classify on what was
thrown, or on what threw it.

**The task's own sentence is the one that produced the fix**, and it came from the brief: *"a hunt
whose instrument also hangs tells you nothing twice."* **Building the instrument before the hunt is
what turned a phantom into a diagnosis in one probe.**

**The dropdown was also mis-stated, the same way.** 11.229 said the label was cut in half *"at the
default text size, live on every device today."* Re-measured in Roboto it **fits — 117 px in a 237 px
box** — and clips from **AX3 (2.35×)** up. Both wrong claims came from the **widget-test font, about
1.6× a phone's**, which `CLAUDE.md` already warns about. Both real defects are fixed: the pulse-modes
header `Row` that bounded only its flexible child and squeezed *"Pulse modes"* to 19.7 px at AX5, and
the dense dropdown boxing its label at one line. **11.229's two Discovered Scope entries and its
Status paragraph are struck and corrected rather than rewritten** — the sequence is the lesson: a
measurement, a resemblance, a conclusion, with only the first checked.

**The instrument's real limit became task 11.233 (Sonnet, below the line).** `clippedTexts` measures
only what a test pumps: **five test files against twenty-six screens.** It has never been wrong about
what it saw and has been silent about the rest, and silence reads as clean. **The brief's own rule is
carried into it — rank before guarding** — plus the instruction that comes straight out of this
task: **measure in Roboto, or a sweep will report thirty clips that are not defects and teach the
next person to ignore the instrument.**

**One Flutter defect is worked around and declared:** `SegmentedButton` throws when asked for a dry
layout, which a `Wrap` inside a dialog does. **The shim's reopen trigger is mechanised as a test**,
so the day it fails the shim is deleted — a workaround that knows when it is no longer needed, which
is the only kind worth having.

**The plan's "four or more pulse modes" is corrected to three** — the model has three slots and
Michael's rule is *"up to three"*, so the acceptance had asked for a state the app cannot reach.

**Stays Partial**, folded into the one look 11.229 is already waiting on.

### Task 11.230 — acted on 2026-09-12 by the planning session; **stays Partial until Michael taps an area**

**The fix is built and the defect it fixed was real, with numbers.** Before the change, with two
overlapping areas on a real temporary disk, deleting one left the survivor at **16 of 20 tiles** and
**3 of 4 elevation tiles**. Both were watched red first. **Michael predicted this from first
principles before anyone read the code, and the code turned out to be worse than his description** —
not only coarse tiles, but every shared tile at every zoom, because there is one file per tile and
nothing recorded which area owned it.

**The status is right.** Every test calls the tap handler with a coordinate; **nothing has pressed a
real screen**, so the tappable-areas acceptance is unproven and the task said so rather than
rounding up. That is the `Done` means a person has looked rule working without being reminded.

**The chooser is the right call and its reasoning is worth keeping.** When a tap lands in two
overlapping areas the app asks *Which area?* rather than guessing. The alternatives were the
smallest (a silent guess exactly where a tap is least likely to mean one thing) or the topmost
(whichever the list happens to end with). **One extra tap, only where areas overlap, and the name of
the area you are about to delete is on screen before you delete it.**

**The best find in this task came from a test that blocked itself.** The download sheet's *"≈ N
tiles"* line built every tile in the selection in order to count them; at the whole-planet framing
the first widget test to open it **died asking for 2.1 GB**. Task 11.103 had fixed this exact thing
one panel over and **wrote in the file that the only caller was the downloader** — false in both
halves: there was a second caller, and it runs *before* the confirmation that was supposed to bound
it. **That is now a rule in `CLAUDE.md`:** write what you searched for, not what you concluded. A
sentence claiming a search was exhaustive cannot go stale visibly, which is the hand-maintained-list
defect wearing a different coat.

**The pre-commit skip was declared, and that is the hatch working as designed** — the hash fill-in
commit touched only `TASK_COMMS.md`, nothing under `lib/` or `test/` changed, and it said so. **An
escape used silently is the hook not existing;** this one was used out loud.

**All three Discovered Scope items became one task, 11.231 (Sonnet).** They are one tool with three
faults, separated only by which line of the file they sit on: the Erase tool still deletes a saved
area's tiles with no neighbour check; elevation coverage counts a tile that *touches* an outline
while Erase removes one whose *centre* is inside, so erasing an area's exact shape leaves its edges;
and `TileSources.byId` answers an unknown id with OpenStreetMap — **the lookup that cannot fail, and
it is what made 11.230's first fixture pass by deleting nothing at all.**

**One decision taken rather than put to Michael, recorded so reversing it is cheap.** Erase will
**subtract saved areas**, like the per-area delete, and report what it kept. The two failures are not
symmetric: erasing too much costs a field download needing a connection the person does not have
where they need it; erasing too little costs disk space and is undone offline in two taps. One rule
in both places is also the simpler app. **If Michael prefers the other option — erase everything,
and name the areas the confirmation will damage — the plan entry says where to say so.**

**Copy recorded in `WEBSITE_PLAN.md`, and it is not red.** There is no offline-data page in the
guide, so nothing drifted. **Noted there: the deleted sentence *"Frees the storage it uses; it can be
re-downloaded later"* was the one that never mentioned the neighbour it was about to damage** — a
guide page quoting it would have been repeating the defect.

**Waiting on Michael, and it is the only thing between this and Done:** open More → Offline Data →
Manage on map and tap inside a downloaded area. The command file stays in place until then.

### Task 11.230 — 2026-09-12 — commit b62b971 — Partial

**What changed, in one sentence:** deleting a downloaded map area now keeps every tile another
area still covers, says how much it will really free before you confirm, and an area has a name
you gave it and can be managed — renamed, re-downloaded, deleted — by tapping it on the map.

**The defect, in Michael's words and then in numbers.** Every tile the app downloads is one
file in one shared folder; an "area" is only an outline in a list. Two areas that overlap hold
the same files. Deleting one area used to walk its outline and delete everything under it —
including the files the neighbouring area still needed — and the neighbour silently dropped to
"Partial". **Measured before the fix, with two overlapping areas on a temporary disk: the
surviving tile area came back 16 of 20 tiles, and the surviving elevation area 3 of 4.** Both
tests were watched red against the old code, then green against the new one. Elevation had
the identical defect and got the identical fix.

**What is built (all tested):**
1. **Delete keeps the neighbour.** The area's tiles, minus every tile any *other* area covers,
   read from the list of areas at the moment you press Delete. Tiles no area claims — the ones
   the map cached while you panned — are fair to delete; they are unowned and come back on
   their own. **That is deliberate, not a gap.**
2. **The number is honest.** The confirmation says *Delete "West block"? Frees 6.0MB on this
   device. Another 4.0MB is also covered by "East block" and stays. Getting it back means
   downloading it again, which needs a connection.* The list row's size is now what deleting
   the row frees, with a second line — *4.0MB shared with "East block"* — when part of it
   stays. The STORAGE totals are read off the disk rather than summed from rows, and a line
   under them says why the rows may add up to less. The snackbar after a delete reports the
   bytes measured as the files went.
3. **Areas have names.** The download sheet opens with *Area 1* (or the next free number)
   selected, so accepting is one tap and typing replaces it. A blanked field falls back to the
   default rather than making an unnamed area. Old unnamed areas still show as *Tile area* /
   *Elevation area* and can be renamed by tapping their row.
4. **The map is the manager.** On "Manage on map", tapping inside an area opens a sheet with
   its name, status, size, and Rename / Update / Delete. **Update adds files and removes none**
   — it re-queues the area under its own id, the downloader skips tiles already on disk, and
   the code says so where the next reader will look. **When a tap lands inside two overlapping
   areas, a chooser lists both and you pick.** Reason, written on the handler: the smallest
   would be a silent guess exactly where a tap is least likely to mean one area, and the
   topmost is whichever the list happens to end with; a chooser costs one extra tap only where
   areas overlap and puts the name of the area you are about to delete on screen first.

**Found on the way and fixed, because it blocked the test:** the download sheet's *≈ N tiles*
line built every tile in the selection to count them. At the whole-planet framing that asked
for two gigabytes and the app would die before you confirmed anything — task 11.103 fixed
this exact thing one panel over and wrote that no other caller existed. Now the bounded
estimate the other panel already used. Recorded in Discovered Scope.

**Also found, recorded in Discovered Scope, not fixed (each a decision or a separate task):**
the map's Erase tool still deletes under a drawn shape with no neighbour check and its wording
does not say a crossed area will drop to Partial; a tile-source id the app no longer knows is

its neighbour by deleting nothing at all; and elevation coverage counts a tile that *touches*
an outline while Erase removes one whose *centre* is inside, so erasing an area's exact shape
leaves its edge tiles.

### Task 11.67 and its follow-up — resolved 2026-09-12 by the planning session

**Done, tested on the device, and the icon it shipped with lasted about an hour.** A person recording
from an aircraft can now say how high the receiver is; the height reaches every bearing and every
no-signal record; it lapses after four hours with nothing recorded and **says so instead of going
quiet**. The Record screen on foot gained one checkbox.

**The design changed mid-task because Michael looked at it, and that is the finding worth keeping.**
The planning session and Michael together specified an altimeter-style glyph, for a good reason —
an aeroplane icon means *radios off* on every phone, which is a terrible thing to hand someone in a
radio-telemetry app in an aircraft. **The reasoning was right and the conclusion was still wrong:**
on the device the gauge was *"too small and hard to tell what it means"*. It is now an **"At
altitude" checkbox**, with the number in the label, and *Irregular/Malfunctioning* shortened to
*Malfunctioning* everywhere to make room. **A small glyph asked to carry a word it has no convention
for is a guess, and only the device settles it** — words are cheaper to read than symbols are to
learn. The plan entry's icon paragraph is struck and dated rather than rewritten, and the test that
refuses `flight` and `airplanemode_active` stays: the rejection still binds anything that replaces it.

**All four measurements came back, and two of them corrected the brief.** Nothing reads
`altitude_agl` — the solver is two-dimensional — **and the viewshed does not read it either**,
though its own doc comment said it did. That comment was false and is fixed; **this task went
looking for readers and found that a document had been asserting one.** Second: with no terrain
tile, the save path had been storing **the phone's GPS altitude as ground elevation** — on foot a
fair stand-in, in an aircraft the aircraft's height written into a column named "ground". It now
subtracts the known height. **Both of those were found by the "enumerate the readers" instruction,
not by the feature.**

**No altitude sensor was added, and that is the rule working.** The brief said a source must be
justified by a measurement; no barometer code exists, and GPS altitude could not be compared against
one from a desk. **So the value is typed.** One fact carried forward: `geolocator` reports altitude
above the **WGS84 ellipsoid on Android** and above **mean sea level on iOS**, tens of metres apart in
places — which is why a GPS-derived prefill stays **offered and unbuilt** until somebody measures it
on a device. Recorded, not scheduled.

**Documents and loops closed by this session:** `TriTrack_Security_Model.md`'s *"returns the day a
person can set it"* paragraph is struck and updated — the column is back in both exports as
`altitude_agl_m`, **zero now meaning on the ground rather than nobody could say**, with the unit kept
in the name because a pilot types feet and the column stores metres. Task **11.30**'s entry carries
the same closure; its reasoning is not revised, its precondition simply ended.

**Handed to the content lane, and it is blocking:** `check_app_quotes` is **red** on two
`Irregular/Malfunctioning` quotes in `recording-a-bearing.md`, so **a website build fails until
`/w-18` runs.** That task now carries the fix, with an instruction to re-read the sentences rather
than swap the token, and to record 11.67's new aerial strings in `WEBSITE_PLAN.md` **without writing
an aerial page** — aerial is rare by Michael's own scope rule and a new page is its own decision.

**Two small things noted, neither scheduled:** `arrival_refresh.g.dart` is stale in git from an
earlier commit that skipped the generator (harmless — the hash only drives hot reload — and the next
generator run will surface it again), and the CSV column is `altitude_agl_m`, which Michael can have
renamed if a script of his expects otherwise.

**Still open for Michael, and it is a look rather than a task:** on a bearing record, do
*Malfunctioning* and *At altitude* sit on one line? The task estimated they fit "with little to spare"
by halving a test-font measurement, **said plainly that it was an estimate**, and made the layout wrap
rather than overflow if the estimate is wrong. That is the honest shape for a thing that cannot be

### Task 11.67 — 2026-09-12 — commit f94897b — Done

**What changed, in one sentence:** a person recording from an aircraft can now tell the app how
high the receiver is above the ground, that height is written into every bearing and every
no-signal record until four hours pass with nothing recorded, and the Record screen for somebody
on foot is unchanged except for one small gauge icon on the position line.

**The four measurements the brief asked for, each as measured or unknown:**

1. **What reads `altitude_agl` today — measured: nothing.** Outside the models, the database
   schema and the two CSV writers that deliberately left it out, no code in `lib/` reads the
   column. **The position solver is purely two-dimensional** (zero references in
   `lib/localization/`), so this was a provenance gap, not a wrong-answer defect. **And the
   viewshed does not read it either** — its doc comment said *"the UI wires this to the
   observation's `altitude_agl`"*, and that was false: the only caller is the Main Map's
   tap-to-predict, which reads a slider on that screen (0–122 m, default 1.7 m). The comment is
   corrected; nothing about the viewshed's behaviour changed.
2. **What `elevation` being required costs an aerial record — measured.** With no terrain tile
   under the position, the save path stored **the phone's own GPS altitude** as *ground
   elevation* — on foot a fair stand-in, in an aircraft the aircraft's altitude written into a
   column named "ground". Now that the height above ground is known, the fallback stores the
   GPS altitude minus that height. Both inputs are real; nothing is invented. Over water with a
   tile, the tile answers as before.
3. **Which altitude source — unmeasured, so none was added.** `sensors_plus` is in the app but
   only the compass uses it; no barometer code exists anywhere. I cannot measure GPS altitude
   against a barometer from here, and the rule is that a source is justified by a measurement.
   **So the value is typed** — a pilot reads it off the panel. One fact worth carrying forward:
   `geolocator` reports GPS altitude **above the WGS84 ellipsoid on Android and above mean sea
   level on iOS**, which differ by tens of metres in places, so a GPS-derived prefill would need
   that settled on a device before it could be trusted.
4. **An aerial flag — answered by Michael, none added.**

**What was built, and the three things the brief left for the task to settle:**

- **Where the icon is: on the position line, beside `Preview/Set`.** Altitude is the third
  coordinate of a position, and this is Michael's own reasoning for that row (*"being adjacent
  to the lat/lon implies position"*). It spends **zero pixels above the fold** on foot. Once a
  value is set, a line at the very top of the form shows it and opens the same sheet, so a pilot
  scrolls to the icon once per flight. **This is a placement judgment — the brief said "on the
  record screen" and no more.**
- **The sticky value survives a restart — yes.** Four hours spans a restart in practice (a phone
  rebooted at a fuel stop; iOS killing the app in the background between passes), and an
  in-memory value would return to zero with nothing said, which is the silent change this task
  refuses. Persisting it is also what makes the window honest across a restart: the four-hour
  rule runs on the stored timestamps at load, so a phone switched on next morning owes the
  *notice*, not the value.
- **The line above the fold shows the number**, not only that one is set: *"Receiver altitude
  300 m above ground"*, in the unit last chosen. After a lapse it reads *"Altitude cleared — was
  300 m above ground"* with a **Restore** button, until one record is saved.
- **The lapse cannot resurrect.** Every mutation in the notifier starts from the resolved state,
  so a save at four hours and a minute clears the value rather than moving its clock. **Watched
  going red** with that resolve removed (expected 0, got 300).
- **MSL refuses without ground elevation — watched refusing** in two cases (no tile under the
  pin; no position at all), and converts by the tile when there is one (1500 m MSL over 1200 m
  ground → 300 m AGL). An MSL figure below the ground is refused too. **The MSL conversion reads
  the terrain tile and only the tile** — never the GPS-altitude fallback, which in an aircraft is
  the aircraft.
- **Non-detections carry the same value**, tested through the screen into the table.
- **Both CSV exports carry the column again, named `altitude_agl_m`** — the `_m` says the unit,
  which matters most on a column a US pilot typed in feet. **The brief said `altitude_agl`; if
  the exact name matters to anybody's R script, it is a one-word change.**
- **The icon is `Icons.speed`, a gauge dial** — the nearest thing in Material's set to an
  altimeter. A test refuses `flight`, `airplanemode_active` and their neighbours.

**Verification:** 10 pure-logic tests, 17 screen tests inside the real tab shell at phone
geometry, the CSV tests, the observations suite (109), the documentation suite, and
`check_app_quotes` (178 quotes, PASS). `flutter analyze` clean.

instead of the base file alone. It was watched failing with the fix reverted, which it had never

check rather than in the thing checked.

the same discarded volume in `docker-compose.e2e.yml` and `docker-compose.dev-lan.yml`, both
carrying the same comment that was true in August and false since 2 September. **That is now task
11.228, Sonnet, low, below the line**, and its brief does one thing the report did not: it refuses
to inherit the report's own sentence *"the same one-line-plus-comment fix would close both."* **An

there** — so the task decides per file, writes the reason into the file, and makes the guard iterate
overlays rather than name one. **An overlay with no recorded decision must fail the guard**, because
this defect got to three instances by passing through omission each time.

**The sweep is why we know the number is three and not unknown.** That is the argument for the
"fix nothing else you find, report the table" instruction, and it should be reached for again.

### Task 11.226 — resolved 2026-09-12 by the planning session

**Done, and the brief was right about the failure and wrong about its size.** It predicted one
mismatch, in the v9 group, for a named reason — the approximating `UNIQUE (tag_id)` task 11.220 added
to keep that group running. **That prediction came true.** What it got wrong was reach: the v6→v7
group's `setUp` strips two versions' additions rather than one, so the oracle had to replay both
migrations; and the v8→v9 group drops `Tag_Versions` entirely, a table v12 and v14 also modify, so a
bootstrap-comparable catalog needed a hand-written catch-up replaying that table's share of two later
migrations. The catch-up is documented beside the test, which is the right place for it.

**That has been written into `CLAUDE.md` as a rule**, because it is a new failure and not a repeat of
the count errors: **a correct number attached to a wrong picture of the blast radius.** The
count-before-deciding rule stops a brief inventing a figure; it does nothing about a brief that gets
the figure right and the scope wrong. The tell is *expect one* with no sentence saying what the fix
touches. **When a brief predicts a failure it should predict its reach too, and mark that half as an
estimate**, so the task knows which sentence to distrust when the work runs long.

**All four migration groups now have the oracle** — v6→v7, v7→v8, v8→v9 and v11→v15 — each watched
failing on a deliberately broken reconstruction and green again once reverted. That comparison is
what caught the v14 defect that could not run against any database; it now covers every reconstruction
in the file rather than the newest one. **v14's history paragraph is trimmed** to the census as its
reason, with `_tagIsClaimedElsewhere` kept as a parenthetical second — the right shape, since the
census looks and the history argument only reasons.

### Task 11.227 — resolved 2026-09-12 by the planning session

**Done, and the upgrade the beta server needs now exists.** A collar in no project that nothing
names is deleted and printed; one that something still names is refused with the naming tables and
their row counts; two-or-more stays an unconditional refusal. **What makes this trustworthy is that
"names it" is read from Postgres's own foreign-key catalog when the migration runs** — not from a
list somebody maintains — and an empty derivation refuses rather than concluding that nothing names
anything. That is the fourth time this project has replaced a hand-maintained list with something
derived, and the first time the derivation refuses to be empty.

**The fixture built from Michael's real census earned its keep on its first run.** Deleting a row
queued the deferred foreign-key checks, and Postgres then refused the migration's very next
`ALTER TABLE "Tags"` — SQLSTATE 55006, "pending trigger events". **A round-five fixture would not
have found that; the census-shaped one did on run one.** This is the standing "count/measure before
deciding" rule paying out a second time inside one task.

**And the migration can now say what it did.** The Postgres driver silently discards `RAISE NOTICE`,
so the deletion would have happened invisibly. `PostgresMigrations.run` prints every returned row and
one line per version. **A check that cannot report is a check that cannot be believed** — same
family as the instrument that cannot fail.

**The four items it left for this session, all four settled:**

1. **`/11-226`'s wording is fixed.** It said "copy the v14 group's `catalogOf`"; that group is now
   `v11 to v15 (tasks 11.187, 11.193, 11.219, 11.225)`. The command file now names it, says why it

### Task 11.227 — 2026-09-11 — commit dfa4385 — Done

**What changed, in one sentence.** The server's schema v14 upgrade — the one that gives every collar
exactly one project — now goes through on a database like the beta server's: a collar linked to no
project and referenced by nothing is deleted and named in the startup log instead of stopping the
upgrade, and the test that proves it starts from schema 11, which is where that server actually is.

**The three cases, and why only one of them is automated.** A collar linked to *two* projects is
still refused, before anything moves — which project keeps the original identifier changes what a
bearing means in an export, and on a server holding other people's records that is a person's
decision. A collar linked to *none* and named by nothing is deleted: nothing referenced it, so
nothing dangles and no device could ever ask for it (sync is per-project on both sides). A collar
linked to none but *still named by something* — a version chain, a bearing — is refused, and the
message says which tables name it and how many rows. "Named by something" is read from the
database's own foreign-key catalog when the migration runs, not from a list, so `Tag_Versions` —
which the census query does not read — is covered, and a search that finds no foreign keys at all
refuses rather than concluding nothing names anything.

**One defect found and fixed by the fixture built from your census.** Deleting a collar queues the
deferred foreign-key checks for the end of the transaction, and Postgres then refuses to alter the
`Tags` table while those checks are pending — which is the very next thing the migration does. It
showed up on the first run of the five-collar fixture and would have stopped the real upgrade with an
error about "pending trigger events". Constraints are now made immediate before the delete, which is
also the better backstop: a referenced collar would fail at the delete itself, by name.

**The upgrade now says what it did.** The Postgres driver silently discards `RAISE NOTICE`, so a
deletion announced that way would have been invisible. `PostgresMigrations.run` now prints every row a
migration statement returns and one line per version applied. On your server the startup log will
show `schema v12: applied`, `schema v13: applied`, then `schema v14: deleted 1 tag row(s) linked to no
project and named by nothing: <its id>` (or `deleted 0 …` on a database with no orphan), `schema v14:
applied`, `schema v15: applied`.

**What a refusal leaves behind on this path, stated because it is not what the brief said.** The
brief says "a refused server is a v11 server." Each version commits separately, so if v14 refuses, v12
and v13 have already landed and the server is at **v13** — still schema major 2, the same major a v11
app speaks, so nothing stops syncing. The tests assert that state exactly rather than "unchanged".

**Documents.** `TAG_COPY_ON_ADD_DESIGN.md` §3.4's *"there is no production data"* is struck, with a
dated paragraph giving the census (five collars, schema 11, one in none — your run on the Ubuntu VM,
2026-09-11) and what the server's migration now does with each case. `SERVER_DEPLOYMENT_PRIMER.md`:
I read §4's container list against the compose files (five long-running plus the one-shot `backup`
— still right) and its "beta drift / data migration" traps; the "real field season" line there is a
hypothetical about beta data surviving to production, not a claim about today, and it now carries
one sentence saying what the database actually holds. C2's "no machine on which this can be
exposed" is about being reachable from the internet, which the census does not speak to; left alone.
The v15 migration's comment in `postgres_schema.dart` cited the struck §3.4 sentence as its reason
and now cites the refusal instead.

**Watched red, all five:** the orphan split removed (census fixture refused instead of deleted); the
derivation made blind to `Tag_Versions` (three refusal tests failed on the wrong error code); the
empty-derivation guard removed; the runner's row logging silenced (three tests failed on the missing
line); v12's default-name `UPDATE` removed (eight tests failed — the v12 expectation is checked on
every path, refusals included).

**Evidence.** `scripts/run_server_tests_docker.sh`: **992 tests, 60 of 60 files, none skipped,
green** (was 989; the migration file went from 15 tests to 18). **There is no CI until 1 October, so
this local run is the only evidence this task will ever have.** The pre-commit `flutter test` also
passed on the commit.

**For the planning session**
1. **Task 11.226 will meet a renamed group.** It says "copy the v14 group's `catalogOf`"; that group
   is now `v11 to v15 (tasks 11.187, 11.193, 11.219, 11.225)` and `catalogOf` is unchanged inside it.
   Update 11.226's wording so the fresh window looks for the right name. Nothing else in 11.226 is

3. **A deleted orphan's id can survive in a "no signal" entry's listened-for list on the server.**
   That column is by standing decision (§5.9(b)) not a reference, so the migration ignores it, the

   ```
   docker compose exec -T postgres sh -c 'psql -U "$POSTGRES_USER" -d "$POSTGRES_DB" -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -qAt -F "|"' <<'SQL'
   SELECT 'orphan', t.tag_id,
          'versions naming it', (SELECT count(*) FROM "Tag_Versions" v WHERE v.tag_id = t.tag_id),
          'no-signal entries listing it', (SELECT count(*) FROM "Non_Detections" n WHERE n.tag_ids_listened_for LIKE '%' || t.tag_id || '%')
   ```

### Task 10.79 — resolved 2026-09-10 by the planning session

**The warning is built and Android's backup door is shut. iOS and macOS are still open, and always
were** — task 11.214.

**Item 2 asked whether the iOS half should get a finding number of its own, and the answer is no.**
The security model already carries L-10 as *"closed on Android and open on iOS"*, and **splitting one
exposure across two identifiers means two closures to remember and a half-open finding under each.**

> **But the report was right that something is wrong there, and it is the title rather than the
> identifier.** L-10 is titled by the *Android mechanism* — *"`android:allowBackup` is absent and
> therefore true"* — **so a reader scanning finding titles sees a platform they have already fixed and
> moves on.** 11.214 retitles it to name the exposure, and requires that nowhere it appears can be
> read as closed while either platform is open.

**Three things went into 11.214 that the ask did not name, and each is a way this class fails
silently.**

- **The flag does not survive the file being recreated.** A fresh install, a restore, or a migration
  produces a new file and the old file's resource value means nothing. **Set on every launch, not
  once.**
- **A flag that reads back is not a backup that excluded it.** Both are worth having and **they are
  two different sentences** — this project has been bitten by collapsing exactly that pair.
- **This app has no custom platform channel at all** — 11.30 removed the last one and 11.66 confirmed
  it — **so this reintroduces a mechanism the app deliberately shed.** Check for a maintained package
  first, and write down the trade-off either way.

**And the verification is a person, so 11.214 writes the row that tells them**: a hardware-section
entry in the release checklist. **A trigger nobody is told to pull is not a trigger.**

### Task 11.212 and its follow-up — resolved 2026-09-10 by the planning session

**The best finding is that the guard's own parser was broken, and the planning session had relayed
its numbers as fact.** `return resolveProjectRole(` sits at exactly the indentation a class member
sits at, so the declaration regex read a *call* as a *declaration*. **Fourteen phantom methods were
invented across the widened scope and thirteen cleared themselves silently**, because they name
classes that really are constructed all over `lib/`. **The true figures are 95 candidates and 3
uncalled, not the 109 and 4 this session wrote into 11.212's brief.**

> **A false positive costs somebody an argument. A false subject that clears itself costs nothing and
> buys silence** — which is why the parser's shape went unquestioned. **The one that did not clear
> itself is the only reason anybody looked.** Now a rule, with its remedy: **exercise a finder against
> a fixture with a known answer, not against whatever the codebase happens to contain today**, which
> is what the fix does.

**Item 3's cause is neither thing either sighting suggested, and the mechanism is the argument.** The
failing line was **the one assertion in that test with no reason string**, which is why two sessions
read a bare `Expected: true`. The wait above it asked only that the header contain `km` — **the
distance, which arrives synchronously with a fix — while the assertion needed the climb and descent
totals, which wait on async terrain sampling.** The wait was strictly weaker than the assertion it
guarded, **so machine load decided the outcome.** **Task 11.210's loud-wait fix neither caused nor
cured it; this was never a timeout.**

**And a second instance of the same shape was found beside it, failing in the other direction** — a
later condition satisfiable by the totals *arriving* rather than by the distance following a new fix.
**A green that measured nothing about the subscription the test exists to check, and nobody had
reported it because it never went red.**

> **The rate is 1 in 10 before and 0 in 20 after — and the report says plainly that the 0-in-20 is
> corroboration and not the argument**, because 0-in-20 against a true 10% rate happens about 12% of
> the time, **which is exactly how this task came to exist.** That is the lesson from 2026-09-09
> landing in the work rather than in a document.

**The offered rule is taken**, and it is the third face of a family already written down: a readiness
check must assert the outcome rather than the mechanism; a wait that can time out must fail when it
does; **and now — a wait whose condition is weaker than the assertion that follows it is a race, not a
wait.** **This is the one that produces an intermittent red rather than a hang or a false green.**

**Two of fifteen call sites were wrong and thirteen are unexamined. That is task 11.213**, and the
task was right not to widen past its stop order.

**Michael's product question is already answered in the follow-up entry: no tag-history screen for
now**, and **the decision is recorded in the code as well as here** — so the next reader of that test
helper finds a decision rather than an open question. **Deleting the row without marking it would have
left "nobody thought about it" indistinguishable from "this was decided against."**

**The brief's DEM figure was wrong and the instruction beside it saved the task.** The planning
session wrote *"z12 terrarium, ≈38 m/px at the equator"* — **that is the resolution of the tiles the

> *a grep tells you a token appears, not what it means* in its most flattering disguise: the quote was

> cost nothing**, and that instruction has now corrected a planning-session figure six times.

**Michael's two decisions, both made with the cost in front of him.**

  relative vertical accuracy, 10 m at 90% confidence** — a real citation. **So `/11-208` is told to
  rewrite the paragraph, not edit the digit**: the new number is a field judgement made *against* that
  specification, and the file has to say so or it will claim a derivation it no longer has. Rolling
  eight-metre knolls were reporting as flat; he accepted some counted noise to see them.
- **Each graph keeps the colour of the line it is a profile of.** The measure tool's went from brand
  green to its dashed line's own stroke without being asked, and he kept it.

### Task 11.204 — resolved 2026-09-09 by the planning session

**The settlement worked, and the report says why it could.** Both texts stated their reasons, and the
reasons turned out to be compatible under one measurement — the largest clear *rectangle* against
floors in both directions. **A rule written without its reason could not have been settled this way**;
it could only have been overruled. The Position map's band is **161.8** at the default text size,
against 49.8 after 11.203 and ~96-105 before it.

higher than recorded — AX3 to AX4 — and nothing on that screen changed to earn it.** The Offline Data
Map's margin grew on every row but the two 11.162 pinned structurally. **Those screens have had more
clear map than the arithmetic credited them with for as long as the instrument has existed.**

> **So every decision made on the grounds that a screen had no room is now suspect**, and item 1 is
> the first confirmed casualty: the Position map refused the *"New map tiles are not arriving"* band
> on a measured 96-against-96, and the measurement was wrong. **A decision recorded with its reason
> can be re-opened when the reason expires; one recorded without a reason cannot** — this is the
> first time that discipline pays out at scale. **The sweep is item 5 of `/11-205`, measure-and-report,
> acting on nothing.**

**Item 1 is decided rather than asked: add the band.** It is *conditional*, so it costs the ordinary
case nothing, and the screen where somebody is deciding where an animal is is the worst place to be
reading a basemap that quietly stopped updating. **Michael can veto it in one commit**; the round trip
was worth more than the risk.

**Item 3 got a rule rather than a shrug.** *"I do not know which it is"* was the right report. **One
observation is not a flake**, and the next step after a single unexplained red is never a hypothesis —
it is to make it reproducible with a stated number of attempts. That is item 0 of `/11-205`, bounded,
with a stop order, and **it is told what has been ruled out and how, and nothing that has been ruled
in** — task 11.181's brief ranked hypotheses and the answer was one it had excluded by construction.

**Item 4 is the one worth remembering.** The closed panel made the map big enough to show that the
observer markers had been clipping their initials **from xxxLarge up, 22 of 38 pixels at AX1, for as
long as they have existed** — invisible to every text-size ladder, because at every split those
ladders measured, the map was too small to clip. **The third defect found on that same badge in ten
days**, and now a standing rule: when a task adds a state, the existing tests are not evidence about it.

### Task 11.203 — resolved 2026-09-09 by the planning session

**Item 1 needed nothing and got the treatment anyway**, which is the point: a rendering bug fixed with
a pixel probe that was **watched red**. That defect was invisible to every test in this repository and
smaller than the harness's own drift, so it would have come back silently. It now cannot.

**Item 2 is the interesting one, and the planning session was wrong about it in a way worth keeping.**

**The brief predicted the two stacked squares would cost the map nothing, and cited rule 4 of this
screen's own MAP SPACE BUDGET** — *a control that fits in a corner cluster costs the clear band
nothing extra.* **The band fell to 49.8 logical pixels at the default text size against a floor of
96**, and 40.0 from xxLarge up.

> **The cause is not a bug.** `clearBandHeight` charges every overlay the subject's full width
> whatever its own width, **and says so in its own doc comment, deliberately**: *a budget that let
> furniture accumulate along one edge "for free" is the budget that produced the defect this
> measures.* **Two texts, each written on purpose, each defensible, flatly contradicting each other
> — and nothing could tell, because until this task every overlay on every screen really was full
> width.**

**That is a new class and it is now a rule in `CLAUDE.md`: a rule written in a document is not a rule
the code obeys, and two documents can each be right and disagree about a case neither has seen.** The
planning session's error was citing rule 4 without asking what enforced it. **The answer was nothing.**

**Michael's decision, given the choice: fix the instrument and keep the squares stacked.** Task
11.204 settles the pair by measuring the largest clear *rectangle* against floors in both directions
— which holds the harness's reason (furniture cannot accumulate for free, because it eats the width)
and rule 4's reason (a corner square really does leave a readable map) **in one measurement, rather
than picking a winner.** Both texts get rewritten; neither survives as it stands.

**The regression requirement was written to outrank the feature**: the new computation must reproduce
the old numbers exactly on every pre-11.203 layout, and every floor whose margin *grew* on any of the
three screens sharing the harness must be named. **A floor that got easier to clear is a finding, not
a bonus** — which is the harness's own warning, turned on the change being made to it.

### Task 11.192 — resolved 2026-09-09 by the planning session

**A "no" that was measured is worth as much as a yes, and this one is recorded so nobody re-opens
it.** `comment_references` came in at **169 violations across 90 files**, all carrying the same
message — *the referenced name isn't visible in scope* — which **cannot tell a genuinely dead symbol
from a live one the file simply has not imported.** Sampling ~20 of the most-repeated names found
**every one live.** Enabling it would mean adding imports to ~90 files to satisfy documentation
cross-referencing, and the noise would be switched off within a week. **Not enabled, and the
reasoning is in the plan entry rather than in somebody's memory.**

**Item 2 — the hole that leaves, and it is now a trip-wire rather than a note.** The lint only ever
saw `[bracket]` references in Dart doc comments. **A prose sentence naming a file, or a
backtick-quoted filename in a comment, is checked by nothing in this repository** — which is exactly
the shape of the `share_column_coverage_test.dart` incident, found by a person reading.

> **"We should watch this" asks a future reader to exercise judgement they will not have the context
> for.** So the disposition names the count, the threshold and the action: **the class stands at two;
> the third instance buys a repository-wide checker for backtick-quoted filenames, not another look
> at this lint.** Written into `CLAUDE.md` as well as the plan entry, **because a threshold that
> lives only in a plan entry is a threshold nobody is standing at.**

**And the sampling paid for itself.** `geo_math.dart` had a doc comment for `distanceAndBearing`
merged onto `ellipsePolygonPoints` since Phase 7 — two functions inserted between a comment and its
subject with no blank line between them — so the comment described parameters that function does not
have, while `distanceAndBearing`, called from six screens, has carried no doc comment for months.
**Cosmetic, and it is still the class this task existed to find:** a reference that was correct when
written and silently falsified by an edit somewhere else.

**The second half held too.** 11.199's guard separates a display from a store *by layer*, and its
author wrote the limitation down rather than hiding it. **The assumption was measured against the
current tree, found true, and is now asserted** — watched red twice, by injecting a `.db` read into
`app_router.dart` and by dropping a widget file under `lib/core/`. The full derivation (*anything
importing `package:flutter/widgets.dart` is a display*) is named as the better rule and explicitly
deferred. **A limit somebody wrote down on purpose is not the failure this project chases.**

### Task 11.199 — resolved 2026-09-08 by the planning session

**The guard found four sites nobody had ever reported, and that is the whole argument for having
built one.** The brief said **two** remained, taken from five reports over nine days. **Six did, in
four files.** The reports were an accurate record of what people happened to *notice*; **they were
never a census, and no number of them becomes one.** **`CLAUDE.md` now carries it: when a defect
shape has been reported often enough to be called a shape, the next task is the instrument, and its
first run is the first honest count.**

**Item 1 — the count is corrected wherever it is quoted.** *Five reports, six sites.*

**Item 2 — the four copy changes are on `WEBSITE_PLAN.md`'s list**, and the four moved baselines are
folded into **`/w-13`**, which is regenerating anyway to prove its own items. **The paste card is the
one to look at**, because it **gained a line** rather than only changing words.

**Item 3 — the decision, and it is a coupling rather than a rewrite.** The guard separates display
from store **by layer**, which is correct today and **quietly narrower than it reads** the day
somebody puts a widget under `lib/core/` or a CSV writer under `lib/features/`. **Its author stated
that limitation instead of hiding it, which is why it can be acted on at all.**

> **Keep the layer rule. Assert the layering it depends on** — `CLAUDE.md`'s write-an-exception-as-a-
> coupling rule — **so the day the assumption stops holding, something says so.** **The full
> derivation (*any file importing `package:flutter/widgets.dart` is a display*) is the better rule in
> principle and a bigger task; explicitly not built.** Folded into **task 11.192**, which is already
> the cheap-static-checks task, **with one instruction that outranks the rest: measure the current
> tree first — if the assumption is already false somewhere, that is a finding.** And **if it cannot
> be asserted cheaply, 11.199's written limitation stands as the answer** — a limit somebody wrote
> down on purpose is not the failure this project chases.

**Item 4 — Michael's to keep or delete, and he has been told.** The paste screen's *"The record's
older signal field says Normal."* is **attributed to the field rather than presented as the record's
mode**, and appears only when the payload has no mode name. **That attribution is exactly right**:
`signal_type` is lossy on a third mode and does not describe a v12 bearing at all, so stating it as
*the record's mode* would be the friendly-word-over-a-column-this-build-no-longer-reads failure the
brief warned about. **One-line deletion if he would rather it never appeared.**

**Item 5 — the guard was watched red five ways** and, run against the morning's tree, **named all six
sites and the stray mapping by file and line.** That is a guard whose first output is a measurement.

**And the honest limit is recorded rather than glossed:** the guard **cannot tell a bad word from a
good one.** A screen showing *Faulty* for a tag stored as `malfunction` passes it, and the mismatch
reaches the CSV. **That still needs a person reading a screen** — the same gap task 11.194 found by
