### Task 11.197 and its three follow-ups — resolved 2026-09-07 by the planning session

**Eleven changes, then three rounds of Michael reading the screen back on his phone.** That is what a
rendering task closing properly looks like, and it is the reason the result is his rather than a
guess about him.

#### The red nobody was told about, and the rule it produced

**`check_app_quotes.dart` is failing on six quotes** — `BEARING QUALITY`, `PULSE MODE`,
`SIGNAL STRENGTH`, *"Preview / set position on map"* on **two** pages, and *"Directional"*. **Five
came from the first commit and were not reported in its entry.**

> **The reason is reusable and is now in `CLAUDE.md`: that check is its own workflow (`website.yml`),
> not part of `flutter test`.** The pre-commit hook was **legitimately green** the whole time and
> nothing said a word. **A task that changes user-visible copy now runs the check itself before
> reporting — it takes about ten seconds.** This is the local-gate-and-push-gate rule with a third
> set in it.

**All six are `/w-15`'s**, and its brief now names them.

#### Three instrument rules, all from the follow-ups, all bigger than this screen

- **Do not animate in response to something that is itself animating.** The reveal animated each
  correction over 180 ms; **the keyboard reports its height on every frame of its rise**, so every
  frame interrupted the animation before it. **Jumping once per frame is what looks continuous** —
  the smooth motion the eye sees is the keyboard's own. **Anything reacting to `didChangeMetrics`
  has this shape.**
- **An assertion made by looking for an absence can pass for reasons unrelated to the change.** The
  first Note test searched for the text of an *unselected* record type — **which finds nothing on any
  record type now that the unselected segments are icons** — **and could not have worked by absence
  anyway**, since that form is a `SingleChildScrollView`. **Two independent reasons for a meaningless
  green in one assertion**, caught only because the numbers beside it looked too small. **Assert by
  position, size or order.**
- **`Scrollable.ensureVisible` is unreliable on a child that has just changed height**, because a
  `SliverList` estimates the extent of children it has not laid out and that estimate is still
  settling. **The working version measures the two render boxes and scrolls by the difference.** And
  **the keyboard's inset reaches the enclosing `Scaffold`s over more than one frame**, so one pass
  landed 48 pixels short — it converges now, bounded at four attempts, and yields if the person takes
  hold of the form. Both are written into the code where the next person meets them.

#### `Directional` → `Bearing` is a ratified exception, not drift

Task 11.194's rule says the displayed word matches the stored word, abbreviated where space demands
it, **so nobody reading their data in R has to learn a mapping.** ***Bearing* for `directional` is a
synonym, not an abbreviation.** **Michael asked for it directly and it is his data.** The stored
value is unchanged, the reasoning is beside the value in the enum, and **the exception is now written
into 11.194's own entry** so the next person finds the argument rather than re-deriving it as a
defect.

#### The triangulation session: retired, and that needed a new convention

**`findBySession` had no callers before this task and has no data source after it.** Its judgement —
**it stays** — is right and is now recorded where task 11.62 will meet it: **it is the only way to
read back rows that already exist on people's devices. It is retired code with a reason, not dead
code.**

**And `PERMISSIONS_MATRIX.md` gains a second convention**, because the removed-capability marking set
the same day does not fit. **Removed** means the code is gone and no row can exist. **Retired** means
**the control that created rows is gone while the rows, the table and the server-side permissions all
remain and still govern what exists.** S1 is marked that way and **describes the surviving half
rather than striking it through**. **The failure being avoided is a reader concluding from silence
that a person can still attach an observation to a session.**

#### The two Discovered Scope findings

**Task 11.198, below the line:** two Tag Database icons — a tag's status badge and the viewer's
padlock — are drawn in the same near-white grey 11.197 just measured as unreadable. **Suspected, not
measured, and the reason is the finding: neither appears in any published screenshot**, because the
seeded state has no badged tag and photographs an owner. **Two states nobody has ever looked at.**
The task is told to measure first and that **a measured "no" closes it properly.** The padlock is
flagged as mattering more — **task 11.184 moved its words to the details page**, so an unreadable
padlock makes that trade worse than it was recorded as being.

**And a warning that goes to both content tasks: the `position` screenshot's diff is not stable.**
**14.56% of pixels on one run, 1.34% on the next, nothing in between touching that screen.** **That
number cannot currently be read as how much the screen changed**, and **no Position baseline should
be accepted on one run.** In `/w-15`'s brief and the plan banner.

#### What is left with Michael, and it is all judgement

Four things he can overrule, none of them defects: **the `?` rather than an X** for No Signal — built
that way deliberately, because an X in a row of five is the standard *cancel* glyph and this control
decides what kind of record gets written; **icon-plus-word on the selected segment** and bare icons on
the other four, which was the recommendation and was taken; **the grey** on the unchecked
Irregular/Malfunctioning label, which may be too faint in daylight; and **eight lines for the Note
box**, which is *"more than the keyboard leaves"* rather than a measurement. **Plus one cost:** the
18pt selected tag loses about three characters of a long name.

conclusion.**

**And the decisive number is not a majority, it is all of them.** 20 requests across 16 tasks handed
an appearance question to Michael, and **20 of 20 were about a change the same task had just made on
purpose** — so a golden's only honest claim, *"this did not change"*, would have been re-blessed in
that same commit. **Zero rendering defects in this project have ever been caught by anything
picture-shaped; every one was caught by a number.** Both recorded in
`TriTrack_Technical_Context.md`.

**The policy is coupled rather than declared, which is the shape now settled on.**
`rendering_verification_policy_test.dart` reads the simulator harness, **so if that harness is
deleted or its accept gate removed the policy reddens and the decision must be made again rather
than inherited.** Watched red four ways.

**Item 1(a) — nothing runs the harness. Not a task: it is now release-checklist item B2, and it is a
human step on purpose.** Its entire value is that the accepting is done by somebody who looked. On a

**Item 1(b) — one text size. Not a code task: it is the content lane's, and it is now the first thing

### Task 11.185 — resolved 2026-09-07 by the planning session

**It asked for nothing and the deviation was implemented as the plan directed.** The sentence lives
in the selection panel beside the ellipse switch rather than greying out the layer toggle, because
that toggle still governs every other wedge on the map. **Michael is being told it is his to
overrule.**

**The Position Estimation screen got a real verdict rather than a shrug, and the numbers are the
reason it is trustworthy:** its wedges never exceed `0.14` fill / `0.3` border whatever is included,
against that screen's ellipse at `0.18` fill and `0.7` border. **It does not have this problem, the
comparison is written into the code, and no change was made there.** That is what a written verdict
is supposed to look like.

**One thing in the report is not quite right and is corrected here rather than left to be
inherited.** It said the harness *"hits real network tile requests that time out unpredictably."*
**No widget test in this repository reaches the network** — `headline_offline_suite_test.dart` pins
that `TestWidgetsFlutterBinding` answers every real request synthetically, and there is a test for
it. What `map_screen_test.dart`'s own header records is the real obstacle and is different: **the
`TileLayer`'s image futures never resolve** under `flutter test`, which is why every map test uses
plain `pump()` and never `pumpAndSettle()`. **The screen renders; what cannot be produced is a
picture of it.** *(An unresolved future and a timeout feel identical from outside — the same
infer-from-resemblance class this file keeps recording, and it cost nothing here.)*

**One process note, and the answer is that it is fine.** This task **deleted its own command file
in the same commit**, calling it *"the established convention."* **It was not** — the convention was
that the planning session deletes a command when it resolves that task's comms entry. **But task
11.179 replaced that habit with a check** (a command file for a `Done` task fails the run), and once
the rule is mechanised it stops mattering who satisfies it. **Deleting it atomically with the change
is better than the habit was**, so it is adopted rather than corrected. **The one thing to keep in
mind:** a task that stops short should leave its command in place, because `Partial` and `Deferred`
are legitimately re-runnable and the check lets them pass.

**And the underlying gap is now task 11.186, below the line.** `matchesGoldenFile` appears **nowhere
in `test/`** — no golden, no screenshot, no image comparison anywhere. **Four rendering tasks have
now ended with "please look"** (11.177, 11.149, 11.166, 11.185), and 11.186 is told to count that
properly rather than trust the planning session's list. **It is a decision task, not a build task:**
a whole-map golden is the brittle case everybody learns to re-bless, a widget-level one is not, and

### Task 11.177, 10.80's second addendum, task 11.178 and two ad hoc entries — all resolved 2026-09-06 by the planning session

#### Task 11.177 — the needle, and two markers nobody could have reported

**The hypothesis was confirmed before anything was changed, which is the whole point of writing it
as a hypothesis.** A 90° turn moved the live needle by up to **10.5°**.

**The brief was wrong about the two markers it told the task to check, and being wrong in the right
grammar is what saved it.** It said `trueNorthRelativeDeg` and `navRelativeDeg` *"use
`liveTrueHeadingDeg`, which is not smoothed at all — say whether those swing."* **They swung by up
to 20.5°, twice the needle.** Had the brief asserted they were fine instead of asking, they would
still be wrong. **This is the standing rule about widening a question rather than answering it,
paying out again.**

**And the reason nobody could have reported them is now a rule in `CLAUDE.md`:** *a marker that is
supposed to move cannot show you that it is moving wrongly.* The needle was reported by Michael
within days because it is meant to sit still. The true-north tick had twice the error and the
intended motion hid it completely. **The still markers are the only ones that will ever complain.**

**The third defect nobody predicted is the one that mattered most and it is not cosmetic.** The
smoother's last frame fell back to a stored value instead of landing on the sample it was easing
toward, and `didUpdateWidget` returns early once the heading stops changing — **so nothing ever
closed the gap.** After a 90° turn the ring sat a permanent **7.5° away from the heading the readout
was printing**: the dial and the number disagreed, and had since task 11.106. **Correctly fixed here
rather than filed.**

**The rename is ratified.** `magneticBearingDeg` → `capturedMagneticBearingDeg` forced both call
sites to be re-read rather than quietly inheriting a new contract. **A compatibility break chosen
over a silent meaning change is the right trade every time.**

#### Task 10.80's second addendum — the refusals are watched without anybody remembering to

**Nothing was asked and the observation is kept.** The four startup refusals now live in
`verify_deployment_refusal_matrix.sh` rather than a new instrument: **17 deployment shapes, 14
refuse, 3 start.** The third of those three is the important one and did not exist before — **a
console configured exactly as `server/README.md` tells Michael to configure it must *start*.**
Without it, all four refusals would be equally well explained by *"the console never lets anything
start"*, which would make them worthless and the written procedure wrong. **That is a positive
control and this project should ask for one every time it asks for a refusal.**

**Recorded where the next task will meet it:** the refusal matrix is now where this project proves
startup refusals, at one line per shape. Nobody should write a second instrument beside it.

#### Task 11.178 and the two ad hoc entries

**11.178 itself needs nothing.** Four decisions made in writing, `allTagsProvider` left alone per the
warning, and the numeric-name check the task asked for **found a real defect and fixed it** —
`"Tag 10"` sorted before `"Tag 2"`, now handled by `naturalCompare` in
`lib/core/utils/natural_sort.dart`, tested directly and through the screen. **`project_setup_screen`
was deliberately left in frequency order and said so**, which is the right kind of scope discipline.

because the app-shell ledger was not updated, **and the commit went in past it.** The trap the

### Task 11.173 — resolved 2026-09-06 by the planning session

**No new tasks, and item 1 is the reason this task is better than the one I wrote.** The brief did
not say where to host the check. **It went into `server-suite.yml` rather than
`gate-instruments.yml`, because the latter is path-filtered** — a commit that deletes a
`run_instrument` line while touching nothing under `server/`, `packages/`, `scripts/`, `proxy/` or
the compose files **would never start it, and that is exactly the commit this check exists to
catch.** `server-suite.yml` has a bare `push:`.
**And it mechanised the reason rather than writing it down: if a future task adds a `paths:` filter
to `server-suite.yml`, the guard fails with a sentence saying why.** That is the rule about prose
triggers rotting, applied without being told. Recorded in Technical Context so the reasoning is not
re-derived.

**Item 2 — agreed, and the half-sentence is added.** `CLAUDE.md`'s delimit-by-the-next-one rule was
phrased about the **last** element; this instance is about **a comment belonging to the next one.**
Splitting a workflow by "up to the next step" made a job's last step swallow **the prose header of
the job below**, which names the variable being searched for — **and the same bug reappeared one
level up in the job split.** Both fixed by stripping comments first, which the `callersOf` function
in that same file already did and neither new split inherited. **The general form is now wider: a
delimiter that does not know what a comment is attaches every element's preamble to its
predecessor — and a preamble is exactly where a human writes the words a parser is hunting for.**
Test the split on the last element *and* on an element with a header above it.

**Item 3 — the right call, keep it, and no I do not want that file's wording.** Leaving *"the
eighteen committed gate instruments"* beside a new row saying 22 would have been actively
confusing, and `.github/workflows/README.md` is the executing lane's file.
**One observation without a task: that number was wrong before anybody noticed, and the gate now
derives it.** A count in prose that a program can compute is a copy in the `SETUP_OWNERSHIP` sense.
**Not scheduled — one number, in one README, that a run now prints.** The trigger is the next task
that touches that file: **make it point at the derived count rather than restate it.**

**Item 4 — this is how an unclosable acceptance item should be left.** The runner cost is measured
at 1.35 s on the Mac and **195 ms in a bare `ubuntu:24.04` container with no Docker, Python or
network** — which doubles as evidence the job needs nothing but bash, grep and a checkout —
**and it says plainly that neither number came from a GitHub runner.** **The step times itself and
prints the milliseconds into the run summary, so the first push converts the estimate into a
measurement without a follow-up task.** Somebody reads it once. That is better than a task, and
better than a promise.


### Task 11.172 — resolved 2026-09-06 by the planning session

**22 of 22, up from 11, and the uncertainty it declared was closed by a second appended entry rather
than left standing.** It stated plainly that its 31 sabotages ran through a coverage-only mode and
that a full live-stack run was still in flight — *"if its result is not appended below, I did not

it work.** Every one of the 48 files under `scripts/` now carries **either** a declaration naming
the gate line that runs it **or** `none - ` and a reason — **and a file carrying neither fails the
run.** A marker somebody must remember to add is a hole that has moved; **this one cannot be
omitted.** Beyond the name it also checks that **the command executed under a name mentions the file
claiming it** (11.171's coupling idea — a name is wording and wording is free), that one name has
one owner, and that **deriving nothing fails.**

**Item 2 — task 11.173, below the line.** The coverage question costs a second and is currently
asked nightly. **11.172 declined to wire it and the reason is the shape of the new task: adding a CI
step is adding another call site nothing guards**, which is the class the last three tasks closed.
**A coverage check protected by an unguarded workflow step is the joke telling itself.** So the entry
says wire it and guard it in the same task or do neither, and reuses 11.171's four assertions rather
than inventing a fourth instrument.

**Item 3 — agreed and recorded.** *A check whose only exercise is a twenty-minute Docker run is a
check whose own failure modes nobody watches.* **31 sabotages at a second each is why this coverage
claim is believable**, and it would not have been affordable at twenty minutes each. The rule carries
the danger and the handling together: that mode prints **"NOTHING WAS RUN"** rather than anything a
reader could mistake for a gate result.

**Item 4 — recorded as a rule, and deliberately not scheduled as a sweep.** *A flag that is always
set in one mode carries no information in that mode.* The wire derivation reported through
`FAILED_ANY`, and **under the self-test every wire instrument is supposed to fail — so the flag is
always 1 and the self-test branch never read it.** The derivation could not fail a self-test run.
**The instance is fixed and the population is narrow, so no task**; the recorded trigger is the next
task that touches a multi-mode script. **The general form is worth more than a sweep would be: a
channel saturated in one mode is silent in it, and that mode is usually the adversarial one somebody
built to find exactly this.**

**And the payoff, in the terms that matter here.** One of the eleven lines that could have been
deleted with the gate still printing PASS is `backup_restore_drill` — **the check that says a backup
can actually be restored.** Michael's beta backups failed silently for eleven days and were found
because he asked. **That line can no longer disappear quietly.**

would have guessed: **the tightest case on the ordinary slider is not a text size at all** — tiles
failing on a new project leaves nine pixels of slack.
**The new rule is about the prohibition, not the premise.** Asserting a wrong premise is a mistake
the executor can correct; **forbidding the correction is one it has to overrule me to fix, and only
a careful one will.** So: **a brief may forbid an approach; it may never forbid a finding.**

**Item 5 — the decline is ratified and its reasoning is now a rule, because it is better than the
reason my brief offered.** Not *"because it is a `Stack`"* — a render object owning all six anchors
could be written. **Because a budget can only say no by taking something away, and this screen has
nothing it may take**: every overlay is a licence condition, a control, or a warning about state.
**The cheapest thing to withdraw is a warning, and a warning withdrawn silently is a worse failure
than the one the budget prevents.** So: before asking for a budget to be enforced, **ask what it is
allowed to take** — and where the answer is nothing, an assertion is the honest ceiling.

**Item 6 is the finding that would have gone on being invisible.** Both map budget tests measured a
**hand-written list of overlay keys**, and the Main Map's legend card is a `Positioned` with **no key
at all**, in neither list — **so the floor was only ever asserted for the state where the legend is
switched off**, and the failure direction is the silent one, because a missing overlay makes the
band read *larger* than it is. The Position screen was missing two, and its comment claimed the
assertion *"is what will notice if you did not"* — **it could not have.** Both now derive the set
from the `Stack`'s own children and **refuse to report a band at all if they derive none**, which is
the empty-result rule from task 11.160 paying off a second time.

**Item 7 — the one hand-kept list left is on the screen where it matters least**, with its reason
written beside it and a red rather than silent failure if somebody converts it. **That is the
fail-closed-with-reasons shape**, and the Offline Data Map's floor is held by structure anyway.

**Item 3 — task 11.167, above the line.** Three `SizedBox(width: 52)` labels on the Log screen with
text that grows inside them: **102 logical pixels tall at 2.0×, 306 at 3.0×.** 11.166 was right that
this is a different class — **a budget nothing enforces never binds; a fixed size always binds, and
pays on the other axis silently.** The entry asks for the row rather than the three boxes in
isolation, and forbids simply deleting the width without saying what alignment it was holding.

**Item 4 — keep it, and thank you for asking.** `scripts/derive_space_budgets.py` is beyond what the
task asked for, **reproduces 11.165's counts exactly, and states its own blind spots in its
header.** It is the answer to "point the next sweep here rather than build a fourth instrument",
which this project has now asked for four times.

### Task 11.159 — resolved 2026-09-05 by the planning session

**Item 5 first, because it is my error and it has a reusable shape.** The brief offered bounding the
*increment* rather than the value, and named one falsifier — a long offline burst. **That was true
and it is not what killed the idea.** The structural answer is that **an insert has no increment**:
a row the server has never seen is inserted, so a delta bound is never consulted on the first push,
**which is the cheapest way to plant the very thing being bounded.** The brief's whole premise
assumed an update. `CLAUDE.md` now carries both halves — a delta rule must always say what it does
about creation, and **naming a falsifier is not the same as looking for them.** A brief that offers
a candidate and one way it could fail reads as stress-tested when it has been stress-tested once.

**Item 1 — task 11.163, above the line and small.** The detector exists and **its only reader is a
console that is off by default.** 11.159 was right not to widen into a 489-line script and right
that this closes the loop. **A detector nobody reads is the next station along from a check that
cannot distinguish success from its own failure.** The entry names the three things besides the
function that must change or the script lies about itself, requires the clean case to read well —
*an operator command whose clean state is noisy trains somebody to skim it* — and forbids changing
the exit status, since §4.30 records rather than refuses.

**Items 2, 3 and 6 — read, checked, ratified, nothing rewritten.** §4.30 is well argued: the pin is
an accepted risk of write access because **the person who can do it can already overwrite or
tombstone the same row**, and what is not accepted is that it happens silently. The exceptions for
editing two planning-session documents were declared rather than assumed, which is now the standing
behaviour. And `revision_anomalies` being a server-only table created by `_ensureServerOnlyTables`
— **no migration, no client change, nothing for a device in the field to chase** — is the right
call, with the rejected alternative reasoned in the file's own header.

**Item 4 — folded into task 11.123, which is the task that exists for exactly this.** The
*Appendix — decision index* has no rows for §4.26 through §4.29, **and 11.159 added its own row plus
a note naming the four missing rather than quietly extending the table.** That is the right
behaviour and it is not a fix. **This one is easier than the five 11.123 already covers, and that is
the argument for doing it: its truth is in the same file** — headings against rows, no code-side
model needed. Task 11.84's enumerator is the precedent and **disagreed with hand-written rows five
times on its first run.** Dropping the table is named as a legitimate answer.

**Item 7 — noted, no copy changed.**

**And the sentence in this report worth keeping is the one to Michael:** rejecting a pinned row would
mean picking a number, and there is no honest one — **a counter of a million pins a record as
permanently as four quintillion**, so any threshold safe enough not to reject real data is far too
high to stop the problem. **Losing a field record is worse than writing a line in a table.**

cannot be a test**, and `CLAUDE.md`'s new rule about mechanising triggers now carries that
exception explicitly: some conditions can only be observed by a person, and the requirement becomes
naming who, when, and what they would see. **It is written beside release-checklist item F1 in
Michael's list rather than left in a report.**

declared it rather than assuming it**, which is exactly the behaviour wanted; `CLAUDE.md` now says

**The words are checked and kept as written.** A hidden tab is not a backgrounded app, and the
difference is what resuming costs — that is the right axis, and it is the one that decided GPS.

### Task 11.158 — resolved 2026-09-04 by the planning session

**It shipped the refusal ahead of the measurement, and the reasoning is ratified rather than waved
through, because the brief said measure first.** The justification is stronger than a count:
**every numeric column on the server is a numeric Postgres type, so a word could never have been
stored in one — that half is structurally zero rather than hopefully zero.** A structural argument
beats a census, and the task said which half it covered and which it did not. **The half that can
be non-zero is the two new floors**, neither reachable through the app.

**Both `unbounded` claims turned out to be false, which is the quiet finding here.** 11.136 declared
`revision` and `triangulation_window_minutes` unbounded and changed no bound's value, correctly.
**`unbounded` is a claim that there is no honest range and somebody looked — and on inspection
neither survived.** Both now have floors.

**Item 3 became task 11.159, below the line, and the entry argues with it rather than transcribing
it.** `revision` has a floor and no ceiling: **a row pushed at revision 2^62 wins every merge
forever and no honest edit can overtake it.** 11.158 flagged it rather than proposing a number, and
was right that any ceiling is a guess about a row's lifetime whose wrong answer strands a row.
**The entry offers a candidate it was told not to adopt: bound the *increment*, not the value** —
the server knows the current revision, so *current + N* is a guess about one push rather than about
years. **And it names what would kill that candidate: an offline burst**, which must be measured
before anything is designed. **It also puts detection ahead of refusal as the default to argue
against**, because refusing wrongly strands data while noticing wrongly costs a line in a log, and
the likelier cause is a client bug rather than malice.

**Item 4 — checked in the file, and it did the right thing rather than the permitted thing.**
11.136's widening explicitly anticipated further vocabulary, so 11.158 could have stayed silent.
It amended §4.13 anyway and **checked itself against the ratifying trigger rather than assuming
coverage**: both new floors are declared on `ColumnSpec` in the shared package, so **there is still
no bound the server enforces that a caller does not already hold.** `number_wrong_type` is
correctly described as the weakest disclosure in the vocabulary — it says a column is a number, and
every client already knows that.

**Items 2 and 5 — noted, nothing owed.** The measurement script is the third artifact naming a flag
`bin/server.dart` implements and is guarded in the same group, watched red. And *"a measurement
that nothing broke is still a measurement"*: the only two tests that moved are the two encoding
11.136's exact claims — the ranged-column count 29 → 30, and the unbounded list losing both
entries.


### Task 11.136 — resolved 2026-09-04 by the planning session

**Items 1 and 2 became one task, 11.158, above the line — and the ranking is about timing, not
severity.** A numeric column holding a string that is not a number is refused by nothing;
`{"latitude": "north"}` validates and is stored. **11.136 was right to leave it and right to say
why** — closing it would newly refuse rows that sync today and nobody has counted them.
**But the entry adds the half 11.136 did not say: the population is the smallest it will ever be.**
The only server is Michael's beta holding his own test data, and every month this waits the count
grows and the migration gets harder. **"Measure first" must not become "defer indefinitely"**, so
the task must write the query, say in advance what it will do with each possible answer, and treat
a near-zero count as a licence rather than a formality. Item 2 (`revision` and
`triangulation_window_minutes` declared `unbounded`) is folded in: same file, same question, and a
negative `revision` reaching the merge engine is the one worth thinking about.

**Item 3 — read, checked, and ratified with one sentence it was missing.** The §4.13 amendment does
not overreach: same one field, on `invalid` only, naming only a column the caller sent, still
validated against `tableSpecsByName` on arrival, and 11.122's honest default still reachable.
**What it did not say is the reason it is safe.** The exception justifies naming a column by saying
the caller composed the row and knows every column in it — **and the same is true of the bounds**,
because `NumericBound` is declared on `ColumnSpec` in `packages/tritrack_sync`, which ships to every
client. **So a range code discloses nothing the caller did not already hold**, and the obvious
objection — that `below_minimum`/`above_maximum` lets somebody binary-search a bound — is answered:
there is nothing to search for. **Verified in the copy rather than assumed: no sentence in
`held_row_details.dart` quotes a limit's number.** The model now also carries the trigger that
would break this: **a bound the client does not hold** — a rate, a quota, a tenant policy — would
put it back inside the clause.

**Item 4 — appended to the content lane's copy list**, which now has two entries. The lane is
paused, so a copy change reported today would otherwise be findable only by re-reading a month of
comms entries.

**Item 5 — noted with approval, and it is the harder thing to get right.** Two tests now assert the
opposite of what they asserted before, **both were correct when written**, and each says so in
place rather than being quietly rewritten. **The property they held was moved to a check that

### Task 11.155 — resolved 2026-09-04 by the planning session

**Item 1 — three corrections to my brief, all measured, all accepted, and recorded as the ninth
instance of the class.** (a) There were **seven** bare checkouts, not eight — `broken-control-check`
has carried `fetch-depth: 0` since the first CI commit. **The brief's count came from arithmetic on
grep matches**: nine checkout lines, two `fetch-depth` hits in a context grep, both attributed to
the file just edited. `CLAUDE.md` already said a grep tells you a token appears, not what it means;
**a count of grep matches is that error with arithmetic on top**, and it now says so. (b) The reason
beside that line — a shallow clone "cannot create" a `git worktree` — was **measured false**, and
the full clone it was paying for is gone. (c) **Clone depth was the wrong axis for all seven**: no
job outside `offline-suite` reads git history at all.

**What survived is the half of the brief that was not an assertion**, and that is the lesson worth
keeping: *ask each job what it reads from its environment, not just how deep its clone is.* **That
widening is what found the two real defects** — a weekly job that could have passed without asking
any of the three map providers, and a server run that could have passed having loaded 2 of its 55
test files. **A brief should widen a question rather than answer it.**

**Item 2 — task 11.156, above the line.** `run_offline_suite.sh` runs a bare `flutter test` and
echoes PASS on its exit code, so **a run that reached a tenth of `test/` is textually a pass** — on
the gate that fires on every push, over the largest suite in the project.
**The judgement call 11.155 correctly declined now has an answer in the entry, and it is not the
obvious one: do not assert the skip count.** A number a person chose is the trap 11.150 named, and
`greaterThan(100)` is what it looks like a month later. **Assert the declared *set* of skips with
reasons** — so a new undeclared skip fails, and a declared skip that stops being needed also fails.
That is the fail-closed-with-reasons shape, available here because the skips are nameable.
**The unmeasured JSON-reporter cost 11.155 flagged as uncertainty is carried into the acceptance**
rather than dropped: measure it, report both numbers, say so if it is material.

**Item 3 — verified in the file, and the generalisation is better than the finding.**
`UNEXERCISED_CONTROLS.md`'s fourth-verdict note now carries it: **"has it run against what it claims
to cover?" is a question about the invocation, not only the checkout.** Both defects here were one
command-line flag and one runner exit code, with no shallow clone anywhere near them.

**Item 4 — done.** The command file is deleted.

**And the risk it stated plainly is accepted as stated.** The full-history clone was removed from
the broken-control check on a local measurement, not a runner one. **If GitHub's git differs the job
fails loudly** — `git worktree add` exits non-zero before any probe runs — rather than passing
quietly, and the file says what to put back. That is the right direction for an unverified change to
be wrong in.

### Task 11.153 — resolved 2026-09-04 by the planning session

**Items 1 and 2 became one task, 11.154, above the line — and merging them is honest because they
are the same object: the refresh lists and the guard that watches them.**
**Part one** is the question 11.153 explicitly left open: it audited the two lists it owned and
asked whether any *other* hand-kept invalidation list has the same hole. **`_afterMembershipChange`
invalidated `myProjectRole` and not `projectRoleForUser`, which is the single line `myProjectRole`
consists of** — so an owner changing a role watched the members list update and the "Your role"
card beside it not, from the same tap, **live since task 11.12.** A hand-kept mirror of something
the code already knows is this project's most-repeated defect (11.14, 11.21, 11.23, 11.45).
**Part two** is the family limit, and **11.153 asked for "a guard or an accepted risk" — there is a
third option and the task is told to take it.** Riverpod exports no way to enumerate a family's
*live instances*, but **the providers on the list can be enumerated**, so asserting that every
family on them is `autoDispose` converts *safe by accident* into *safe by assertion*. If that
cannot be expressed, the accepted risk must be recorded **where somebody adding a provider will
meet it, not only in a doc comment on a class they are not editing.**

**Item 1b — the correction is now quoted inside task 11.151's own entry**, per the request that it
be visible to whoever reads that task. `refreshTagViews(projectId: null)` meaning "only the global
list" was **sound about links and wrong about rows** — `projectActiveTags` returns whole `Tag` rows,
and the edit dialog offers no project — so every rename left the Record screen's wheel showing the
old name. **A correction that quotes what it corrected is findable as the error**, which is this
project's rule for exactly this.

**Item 3 — that was my error and it is recorded as the seventh instance, with what makes it
different.** The brief asserted the refresh cost would land *"including every bearing saved"*. **A
bearing saved never reaches `DataArrival`** — it bumps the revision directly. **This one was a
quantity rather than a mechanism**, and `CLAUDE.md` now says why that is not the harmless direction:
an overstated cost argues for caution the evidence does not support, and a task that believed it
would have built something more complicated than the problem. **Numbers in a brief are assertions
about the code and get checked like any other.**

**Item 4 — recorded so nobody measures it again, and so no brief argues from a cost nobody took.**
`TriTrack_Technical_Context.md` gains *What a Whole Arrival Refresh Costs*: median 15.4 ms, the four
gating providers 1.5 ms of it, frequency per sync round that changed rows rather than per write.

**Item 5 — checked in the file rather than accepted from the report, and it is better than what it
replaced.** The deadlock entry now records **three** outcomes, not one — a `keepAlive` provider
hangs silently, an `autoDispose` provider throws, and a watched provider recovers — **so the hazard

### Task 11.151 — resolved 2026-09-04 by the planning session

**The cause was established and the rejected candidate was named, which is what the brief asked
for and what the last two tasks got wrong.** Three providers hold "which tags does this project
have", and **each write site picked its own subset by hand — no two picked the same one and not one
picked all three.** The route Michael actually used picked **none**. The provider-derives-from-
provider candidate was ruled out on evidence: both providers derive only from repository handles,
and the failing test showed a stale cache rather than a rebuild fault — the counter moved and the
value did not.

**Item 1 — task 11.153, above the line.** A tag link, membership change or project rename arriving
on a **sync pull** still refreshes nothing. **This is the worse half of the same defect**, because
the person it fails is not the person who acted: an owner promotes you, your device syncs, and the
Record screen still refuses your bearing until you restart, with nothing on screen saying why.
**The beta is a real team, and this is the failure mode of a real team.**

**Item 2 — the deadlock warning is carried in three places, because it would have closed 11.153
wrongly in ten minutes.** The obvious remedy — those providers watching `recordingsRevisionProvider`,
which `DataArrival` already bumps from inside the merger — **orphans a provider's in-flight `Future`
when a bump lands during its own build, and the app hangs.** Reachable in production, since
`currentUserProvider` announces when it auto-creates a user. Measured: eleven seconds green became a
run that never finishes. **It is in 11.153's entry, in its command file, and now as a standing fact
in `TriTrack_Technical_Context.md`** — the third of those is the one that survives 11.153 being
closed. The safe direction is a listener invalidating from outside any build, **written as a
direction to establish rather than a design to inherit.**

**Item 3 — agreed, and the second half is the better half.** `CLAUDE.md` gains: a guard that greps
for a literal call cannot see through a function call. **And the part worth more than the rule:
11.151's own first self-check for the new idiom scanned the whole file and passed with the helper
gutted**, because another entry point's bump satisfied it. Scoped per function, both gutting
directions confirmed red. **A check written to protect a new idiom must be tested by breaking that
idiom** — scanning the file an indirection lives in proves the file, not the call.

**Item 4 — noted, nothing owed.** All eight local routes go through `refreshTagViews`; recorded in
Technical Context beside `_afterMembershipChange`, with the note that **the sync merger calls
neither** — which is precisely 11.153.

**One process note, recorded because it nearly cost something.** This task was reported complete
while its work was uncommitted and its comms entry unwritten; a mid-work draft of its plan status
said sync arrivals *were* fixed, and the finished report says the opposite and correctly. **The
planning session read the draft, said so, and wrote nothing** — which is the rule about uncommitted
work in a shared tree doing its job. **A status line edited before the commit is a claim about work
that does not exist yet.**

### Task 11.143 — resolved 2026-09-04 by the planning session

**Item 5 first, because it was the dangerous one, and it had a second half nobody saw.** The
staging rule in `CLAUDE.md` is amended: **staging by name is not enough, the commit must name its
paths too** (`git commit -- <paths>`), because a pathless `git commit` publishes the whole index
including whatever the other window staged before you started. That is exactly what `4c262dd` did.
**But the repair created the mirror hazard.** 11.143 restored the planning session's staging
"exactly as it was" — correct in itself, except that the planning session had *committed* those
files in the meantime, so the restored index was a pre-commit snapshot and **any pathless commit
would have reverted work already in history.** It was still sitting there when this was resolved;
the index is now cleared. **The rule therefore says both halves: name the paths on commit, and if
you must clear the other window's staging, say so and leave it cleared.** A stale index is worse
than an empty one, and nobody's staged state is worth reconstructing across another session's
commit.

### Task 11.61 — 2026-09-03 — commit cd0e7b4 — Done (part 1) / Not reproduced (part 2)

**For the planning session**

1. **Mark 11.61 part 1 Done and part 2 "not reproduced, left open" — the entry is already

   mechanism is real: `test/features/more/device_list_reload_loop_test.dart` breaks the identity
   comparison and the loop appears — 13 fetches across 25 pumped frames, in the real shell at
   phone geometry. **The app does not reach it.** In the state Michael described (signed out
   from the Mac, on the Server Connection screen, nothing touched) the screen asks once and

   consistent with the measurement: `CurrentSession` is `keepAlive`, **nothing in `lib/`
   invalidates it**, and every other way its value changes is a genuinely different value —
   including `null`, which converges because `identical(null, null)` is true. **The file is left
   behind as the instrument**: if the freeze happens again, the first question is whether the
   count rises, and something now answers it.
2. **The brief's own premise about the four `.timeout()` call sites was wrong, and this is the
   sixth time a task entry has asserted a mechanism the code did not have.** It said
   `join_request_watcher.dart`, `project_setup_screen.dart`, `map_screen.dart` and one in
   `server_config_screen.dart` "already time out by hand". **Only one of the four was about a
   request, and even that one bounded a queue rather than a request.** The other three: a GPS
   fix, an isolate computation, and a doc comment stating that no timeout existed. **All four
   are handled** — the queue one deleted (its own note said it existed only because requests
   could not time out), two kept with the reasoning written beside them and on a checked

   finding**, and the entry was written from the previous task's report rather than from the
   files.
3. **Three Discovered Scope entries were appended to Phase 11, and one of them is a real
   decision somebody should make.** (a) A sync **push whose upload stalls** is bounded by a
   five-minute total on Android, Windows and Linux rather than by inactivity —
   `package:http` gives no portable hook into a request body as it drains. iOS and macOS do not
   have this gap. Closing it means owning a `StreamedRequest` re-implementation on the path
   every push takes, to shorten one failure by four and a half minutes on platforms Michael does
   not use; **recorded rather than done.** (b) `cupertino_http` 3.0.2 does not expose
   `timeoutIntervalForResource`, so there is no native total-resource ceiling on Apple — noted as
   a fact about the package, not a gap. (c) `UNEXERCISED_CONTROLS.md` names
   `project_setup_screen.dart:422` as the GPS-fix timeout; **it is at line 450 and was before
   this task touched the file.** That table is read as a list of things to go and exercise, so a
   stale line number sends the reader to the wrong place. **Not corrected here** — that survey
   is somebody else's document, and a code task rewriting its numbers is how two documents start
   disagreeing. **Ask whoever owns it to fix the one number.**
4. **A fifth unbounded path was found that no task had listed:
   `cached_tile_provider.dart`'s `http.get` — every basemap tile the map draws.** Task 11.36
   measured the sign-in client and the sync transport; this one is neither, and it is worse than
   it looks, because a hung tile fetch also leaves the tile-health band task 11.135 built
   **silent** — that band is only ever told about a *failure*. Fixed here. **Worth knowing when
   the next "we measured every X" finding lands**: 11.36's measurement was accurate about what
   it measured and was read as covering more.
5. **User-visible copy: none changed, and that is the headline.** The whole argument for this
   task was that the honest sentences already written become reachable once a request can fail.
   A timed-out request renders exactly as an unreachable server does, on every surface. **The
   website lane's drift check should stay green** — nothing in `lib/` gained or lost a sentence.

**For Michael**

1. **Nothing to run, nothing to decide.** The work is committed on `main` as `cd0e7b4`; push
   when convenient.
2. **What is now true on a phone:** if a server accepts the connection and then goes quiet, the
   app gives up after **30 seconds** for anything small (signing in, the device list, join
   settings, a map tile) and after **5 minutes** for one page of sync — and then says so, using

3. **What you will notice that is slower:** a failed sync now waits **fifteen minutes** before
   trying again at the default cadence, because task 11.59 made your chosen frequency a floor on
   retries. That was already true of every other failure; timeouts just join it. **"Sync now"
   ignores it, as always.**
4. **What you will notice that is worse:** a server that is silent for a full thirty seconds and
   then fine within the next thirty used to be ridden out invisibly by the automatic retry. Now
   you see the failure and tap "Try again". That trade is deliberate — a minute and a half of a
   still screen is indistinguishable from a frozen app, which is the thing this task exists

### Task 11.115 — 2026-09-02 — commit ed67126 — Done
**For the planning session**
1. Item B closed rather than implemented: a device-connectivity check cannot reliably
   distinguish "no signal" from "the server is off" on this app's platform set, because
   iOS's and macOS's `NWPathMonitor` can't make that distinction at all (only Android's
   validated-connectivity API can). The reasoning is written into `lib/data/sync/sync_failure.dart`
   and the DEVELOPMENT_PLAN entry. Nothing to decide — flagging so the closure is visible
   rather than silent, per the acceptance criterion that a "cannot be told apart" finding
   still needs to be written down and accepted.
**For Michael**
1. Nothing — this is complete. Item A (the sign-in screen's waiting sentence) shipped; item B
   (telling "no signal" from "server is off" apart) was investigated and closed as not reliably
   possible on iOS/macOS, so "Offline" still covers both — same as before, now with the reason
   on record.

**Resolved 2026-09-02 by the planning session.**
1. **Ratified, and the closure is the right one — with one sharpening added to the plan entry so
   it does not read as "impossible" to a later reader.** It is not impossible; it is **possible on
   one platform only.** Android's `NET_CAPABILITY_VALIDATED` genuinely probes for a working route;
   `NWPathMonitor` reports "satisfied" the moment an interface is up. **So the real choice was
   between one honest word everywhere and a better answer on Android sitting beside a
   worse-looking non-answer on iOS — for the same situation, in an app whose two beta devices are
   one of each.** One word everywhere is right, **and writing it down as a design decision rather
   than a platform limit is what stops somebody re-opening it the first time they read the Android
   documentation.** Reopen triggers recorded: iOS gains a route-probing API, or the app becomes
   Android-first.

**And investigating the platforms rather than reasoning about them is why this closure is worth
anything.** *"Cannot be told apart"* asserted from a desk would have been a guess with the same
words; measured against three platform APIs, it is a finding — and the acceptance criterion that
a negative answer still has to be written down and accepted is what made the difference visible.

   that stop it being re-litigated: **the server answers an identical `202` whether it sent, filed

   halves of 11.115 are now one question asked twice — *the app cannot know, so what does it
   say?* **The constraint is written in as the task itself: the sentence has to be true during an
   outage and true on an ordinary day, because the screen cannot tell them apart.** And it is

   so; **a tool whose silence could be misread is worth one sentence of warning beside it.**
3. **Endorsed, and the exception is stated the right way round.** The standing rule is that a
   summary written to save somebody a lookup becomes the memory and goes stale — **and a worked
   example that names its authority is the legitimate form of that.** `server/README.md` quotes
   the output as an example and `degradation_record.dart` is the authority; keep it that way.
4. **Both halves ratified, and the second one deserved its argument.** A per-event breakdown was

   database the failure is not selective — nearly everything is refused — so a breakdown
   distinguishes very little**, while every dimension added to a record living outside the
   database is a step toward reconstructing activity outside §4.7's rules. **Naming nobody is
   right for the same reason.** **Reopen trigger, and it is a real one: a degradation that is
   *partial*** — some operations failing while others succeed. **At that point a breakdown starts
   to mean something**, and the trade changes. Not a code review.

**And the sentence in your report to Michael is the honest summary of what this task did and did
not do:** the record answers *"was sign-in broken on Tuesday"* for somebody who already suspects

first being where a warning goes when a backup stops (task 11.78 item 6) — and it is recorded as
covering two things rather than one.

### Task 11.124 — 2026-09-02 — commit `970ec23` — Done

**For the planning session**

1. **The task's brief was wrong about one mechanism, and I made the judgment call rather
   than stopping. Please confirm it.** The brief said storing the refusal code needs *"a new
   column on `Sync_Held_Rows`, a `latestSchemaVersion` bump, and a migration step."*
   `Sync_Held_Rows` is a **client-only** table — it is not in `tableSpecs`, it does not move
   with `latestSchemaVersion`, and `SyncHeldRowStore.ensureTable` creates it on every open
   rather than a numbered migration doing it. `latestSchemaVersion` is the *shared* schema
   version negotiated with the server on every request, so bumping it would announce a change
   to the synced tables when none happened. **I added the two columns in place inside
   `ensureTable`, following `UnknownColumnStore.ensureTable`'s precedent from task 10.76, and
   left `latestSchemaVersion` at 11.** Additive rather than 10.76's drop, because a held row
   is the memory that field data has not reached the server. The populated-database upgrade
   test the acceptance asks for is `test/data/sync/held_row_issue_code_test.dart` — same
   obligation, different mechanism.

   `test/data/schema_v9_migration_test.dart` passes on first write. **If a future task expects
   corrected instruments to find something, "they did not" has to be acceptable** — 11.118's
   rule.

3. **The database re-open triage is closed as harness-only.** Nothing real can reach it: the
   app opens its database once per process from a `keepAlive` provider, `PreMigrationBackup`'s

   file** — there is no in-app restore, and every filesystem delete in the app targets map
   tiles, DEM tiles, keychain entries or old pre-migration snapshots. About eight minutes.

4. **A choice I made that the brief did not ask for, so it is worth a look: the wire carries
   the offending column's *name* as well as the code.** Without it the best sentence available
   is "one of the text values in this record", and the payoff the brief describes — *"the
   first name has a character the server will not store"* — is not reachable. The disclosure
   argument is that the client composed the row and already knows every column in it, so the
   server is naming the client's own field back to it. It is still treated as untrusted:
   `HeldRowDetails` matches it against `tableSpecsByName` for that table and falls back to
   11.122's default when it does not match, with a test for a field name that is real on a
   *different* table.

5. **Two Discovered Scope items are now closed and I have marked them** — 11.122's "telling
   somebody which part was refused" and 11.96's `SyncSchedule` hand-rebuild.

6. **Ask for a task if you want it: `RowIssueCode` currently covers only text bounds.** A
   range failure (latitude 999, a frequency outside the VHF window) carries no code and lands
   on the honest default. That is deliberate — those checks are written inline and have no
   declared bound to derive a code from, so coding them would mean typing codes at each
   check, which is the hand-maintained list this design exists to avoid. **The way to widen it
   is to give the range checks a declared bound the way `TextBound` is declared, not to add

   argued itself out of unifying them.** The tidy answer is one constant. **The better answer is

   prediction the app renders **as fact over real terrain** — so rounding the prediction up to 40

### Task 11.96 — 2026-09-02 — commit 914c7a0 — Done
**For the planning session**
1. The sweep 11.117's brief asked for found one more instance of the same bug class, not fixed
   here: `SyncSchedule` (`lib/data/sync/sync_schedule.dart`, 5 fields) hand-rebuilds itself in
   five methods (`recordAttempt`, `recordSuccess`, `recordFailure`, `withFrequency`, `resumed`)
   the same way `SyncStatus` used to. Recorded in Phase 11's Discovered Scope — please give it a
   task number applying the same `copyWith` fix.
2. One deliberate behaviour change shipped alongside the mechanical fix, not asked for by either
   task's brief: `setFrequency`'s old rebuild silently reset `running`/`progress` to false/null
   on every call (even mid-round), which the neighbouring `dismissStaleness` rebuild never did.
   `copyWith` makes the two consistent by carrying both through — more correct, but worth a
   planning-session sign-off since it changes what the sync bar shows if someone taps the
   frequency control while a round is in flight.
**For Michael**
1. Nothing — this is complete. No app behaviour changed except the one item above (the sync bar
   no longer flickers to "not syncing" if you change the sync-frequency setting while a round is
   actually running).

**Resolved 2026-09-02 by the planning session.**
1. **Folded into task 11.124 as its first item, and the placement is the point rather than
   tidiness.** **11.124 adds a field to the sync layer.** A hand-written five-method rebuild is
   exactly what makes adding a field dangerous — every argument supplied, every one valid, and
   **the compiler cannot say that one call site forgot the new one.** For `SyncStatus` the silent
   default meant *healthy*, the calmest possible lie. **So: `copyWith` on `SyncSchedule` first,
   then the field.** Third instance of this class in the same subsystem, and the first one to be
   removed before it could bite rather than after.
2. **Signed off — and verified rather than accepted on your description.** The planning session
   read `setFrequency`: it writes the store and rebuilds the status and **does not cancel a
   running round.** So the round really is still in flight and the old reset was **the sync bar
   making a false statement about the app's own state** — which is the defect tasks 11.114 and
   11.116 spent themselves on, arriving by a third route that needed no restart, only a tap.
   **Correct as shipped, and shipping it beside the mechanical fix was right**: `copyWith` is what
   made the inconsistency visible, and leaving the two rebuilds disagreeing would have left the
   next reader to discover it. **Reopen trigger recorded:** if `setFrequency` ever gains the power
   to cancel a round, `running: false` becomes true again and this must be revisited.

5. **A risk that was already there and is now written down:** the map tiles may be being
   fetched with a `User-Agent` OpenStreetMap's policy says they will block. I have not
   confirmed it either way. If your basemap ever goes blank for no reason, this is the
   first thing to check.

**Resolved 2026-09-02 by the planning session.**
1, 2, 3. **One task — 11.134 — because they are one exposure: this app depends on three
   third-party tile services under published terms, and nothing in the app or the suite checks
   that it still complies with any of them.** Two items are compliance, one is availability, and
   **all three fail silently**, which is what makes them the same task rather than three.
   **Item 1 goes first and puts 11.134 above the line**: a `User-Agent` block arrives as tiles
   that stop loading, which the app reports as nothing at all, on the one screen a field
   technician uses all day. **The task is told your own framing — find out what is actually sent
   before designing anything** — and it carries a second question that survives whatever the
   answer is: *what does the app say when tiles stop arriving?* Today, nothing, and a blank
   basemap from a block is indistinguishable from a blank basemap from no signal.
   **Item 3 is decided rather than researched: add it.** You could not settle whether direct
   raster access triggers "Powered by Esri", **and the cost of being wrong is asymmetric** — four
   words, allowed behind a button, and App Info and the ⓘ are already exactly that. **A question
   that costs more to answer than to satisfy should be satisfied**, which is now a standing rule
   with the caveat attached that it is not licence to skip research where the obligation is large.
4. **Recorded in `CLAUDE.md`, and it is the kind of thing that would have cost somebody an
   afternoon.** Savings from padding and tap-target constants are exact; **savings from joining
   two facts onto one line are understated, sometimes to zero**, because the joined line wraps in
   a test font about twice Roboto's width. **So a layout change that reads as "no improvement" in
   a widget test may be a real improvement on the device** — and the two kinds of saving must
   not be reported as one number.

**And the judgement this task is most likely to be second-guessed for is the right one.** The
Terrain credit bar is the same size as before because **OpenTopoMap's terms say the credit
*should* be visible rather than *must*, and the licence they link is an older version with no rule
about putting text behind a button.** Leaving it whole is exactly what the brief asked for when
unsure, and *"only one of three got shorter"* is the honest outcome rather than a half-finished
one. **Reading all three providers' terms and giving three different answers is the result** —
one answer for three would have been the failure. The Maxar → Vantor correction found along the
way is the proof: **the credit was already wrong, and nothing would ever have said so.**

### Task 11.128 (follow-up) — 2026-09-02 — commit `f9164f4` — Done

**Plain English first.** Michael asked for item 4 of the previous entry: the server had no
health check at all, so `docker compose ps` said nothing about it. It has one now. A server
whose database is unreachable still reports **healthy** — on purpose, because "unhealthy" is
the label a restart hangs off and restarting cannot reach a database that is down — but the
health log now carries a sentence saying sign-in is dead and which address to ask.

**For the planning session**

1. **A Discovered Scope entry I wrote three hours earlier was wrong, and building it is what
   caught that.** I had said a health check would let `restart: unless-stopped` restart a
   process that is alive but wedged. **It does not.** Docker Engine's restart policies react to
   the container *exiting* and do not act on health at all — that is a Swarm/Kubernetes
   behaviour, and this stack is neither. Measured: a container forced unhealthy sat at
   `Up (unhealthy)` for as long as I watched, same process id, restart count still zero. The
   entry is corrected in place with the measurement, and the claim shipped in the code and the
   README is **visibility, not recovery**. **Worth noting as the same shape as the finding this
   whole task started from** — an assumption about a mechanism nobody had run. No action needed
   beyond knowing the corrected entry is there.
2. **Nothing new to raise.** The two items from the previous entry — the red documentation
   test whose remaining offender is `.claude/commands/11-125-…md` line 106, and the missing
   record when the database dies underneath a running server — are unchanged and still yours.
3. **One thing worth reusing: `server/test/security/shipped_defaults_test.dart` now asserts a
   compose file's `test:` string against the flag `bin/server.dart` implements.** That is
   task 11.125's "a harness that patches a named line is coupled to code it does not own"
   class, in a new place — a rename of the flag would not fail loudly, it would leave a
   container reporting unhealthy forever with nothing saying why. **If a future task needs the
   same guard for another compose command, that group is the pattern**, rather than a fresh
   one-off.

**For Michael**

1. **You said you can restart the server, and you will need to** — the health check only exists
   in a container built from the new image, so `docker compose up -d --build server` on the VM
   when convenient. Nothing breaks if you don't; the service simply keeps reporting no health,
   exactly as it does today.
2. **After that, `docker compose ps` will show `(healthy)` on the server.** If you ever want the
   fuller sentence — the one that says whether sign-in actually works — it is:
   `docker inspect -f '{{json .State.Health.Log}}' <container>`, or just
   `curl -i http://localhost:8080/ready`.
3. **Do not read `(healthy)` as "everything is fine".** It means the process is running. A
   server that cannot reach its database reports `(healthy)` too, deliberately. `/ready` is the
   one that knows the difference, and the health log spells it out.
4. **Nothing automatic will restart anything.** I checked this rather than assuming it, and it
   is the one thing I would not have guessed: Docker will not restart a container just because
   its health check fails. The health check makes the state visible; it does not act on it.

   before the restart; with it everything works, which I confirmed. Steps 1 and 4 also have no

   come before it — so the only way Michael starts this server could not be run through it, so
   the ownership fix it exists to apply never applied, so the beta host's backup scheduler ran

   hoisted, and the script prints the scheduler's uid beside the `backups/` directory's owner

   typing, the scheduler ran as uid 70. Header corrected — a disagreement now means *the

   other "these two cannot disagree" claims in this repository; I checked only this one and

**Not a numbered task.** Michael was asked which of three options to take on task 11.119's

**USER-VISIBLE COPY CHANGED — three strings on the sign-in screen.** `EMAIL ME A SIGN-IN CODE`
became `REQUEST A SIGN-IN CODE`; *"Check your email, then paste the code below."* became *"A
sign-in code was requested. Paste it below once you have it."*; the field helper *"Paste the
code (or the whole link) from the email"* became *"Paste the code, or the whole link"*. A new
sentence appears after a request, explaining that delivery depends on the server. **I checked:
`website/` quotes none of the three, so the drift check is unaffected** — but the content lane
should know, because the sign-in flow is guide material.

**For the planning session**

1. **The literal instruction could not be met, and the reason is worth carrying.** *"Say how

   the identical `202` whether the code was emailed, written to a file, or discarded, **because
   §4.5 requires it to.** The app has no way to know. So the copy is honest about not knowing
   and names an action instead. **Michael was told this before choosing**, and picked the
   screen-only option over teaching the server to report its delivery method.

   Writing *"this server does not send email"* would be specific and true of every deployment
   that exists. It would also be **false on every already-installed build the day somebody adds
   a mail sender** — the exact correct-when-written-then-silently-falsified class task 11.119
   surveyed. **A client must not hard-code a fact about a server it ships separately from.**

   have to report its delivery method on the sign-in response; that touches
   `auth_routes.dart`, which the Broken-control workflow watches, and it needs a disclosure
   decision — telling an unauthenticated caller that a server has no mail sender is a property
   of the deployment rather than of any account, so I believe it is below the §4.13 bar, **but
   that is my reading and not a verdict.** Only worth opening if somebody builds SMTP.

   `test/documentation/sign_in_delivery_vocabulary_test.dart`, beside 11.98's invitation one and

   to do instead of a fresh one-off grep.** It is scoped to *delivery phrases*, not the word
   "email": the word is legitimate all over the app (the field label, stored addresses,

   hat, which is 11.89's rule. Its survivor list is empty and it matches zero string literals

5. **It was watched failing before being trusted.** I restored the old helper text, ran the

### Task 11.97 — 2026-09-01 — commit d993e51 — Done

**What changed, in one sentence.** The app used to build a connection to its server in three
separate places, and none of them could be pointed at a pretend server, so eleven of the
fourteen things the sync bar can say could only be seen by a person holding a phone; it now
builds that connection in one place, and a new test file makes a pretend server behave badly
in eleven different ways and checks the exact sentence the bar puts on screen each time.

**The result, which is not "the connection is now replaceable".** Every one of those eleven
tests was first run against the old code. **Nine failed, and all nine failed identically:
the bar said "Offline".** That is the whole finding. With the engine building its own
connection, substituting a server did not give you a *failing* server — it gave you *no*
server, so the only two states any test could ever reach were the two that describe a request
that never arrived. **No state, once reachable, turned out to be wrong.** The bar was right
about all eleven, including the four that tasks 11.54 and 11.60 had to fix from real
hardware. They are now held in place by tests instead of by memory.

**Three states are still not driven from a server, named rather than left blank.** A refused
server address is decided before any connection is built, so no substituted server is
consulted (it is driven by `server_address_refused_test.dart`); the two "not synced in N
days" states are facts about a clock rather than about a server (driven by
`sync_provider_test.dart`). The test file's header carries the full table.

**For the planning session**
1. **Nothing is blocked and nothing needs re-scoping.** This task is complete as written.
2. **The content lane can now photograph the sync bar's failure states, and should be told
   which override to use.** `/w-05` said the screenshots follow once the seam exists — it
   exists. The override to reach for is **`serverTransportProvider`**, which replaces the
   connection everywhere including the sync engine; the harness's existing
   `membershipTransportProvider` override still works and still covers membership only, which
   is why `joined.dart`'s statement that the sync engine is never faked is still true. Ask
   the planning session to put that sentence in the next website task rather than leaving it
   to be rediscovered.
3. **`integration_test/screenshots/joined.dart` was deliberately not touched** (this task's
   boundary), so its comment explaining that `SyncController` "builds its own HTTP transport"
   is now out of date — the mechanism it describes is gone, though the behaviour it relies on
   is unchanged. That belongs to the content lane to correct, not to a code task.
4. **A test-harness trap worth a standing note, because it cost most of this task.** Three
   separate hangs, each a ten-minute timeout with *no output at all* rather than a failure,
   all from one cause: **anything that reaches SQLite must not be awaited inside a
   `testWidgets` body.** A widget test runs on a fake clock; awaiting a real database answer
   outside `runAsync` leaves that clock's pump loop dead, and every later `pumpWidget` hangs
   forever. The same rule bit a third way — a `Completer` created in the test body remembers
   the fake clock and resumes its listeners there, so the round it was gating never finished.
   **A test that hangs is worse than one that fails**, because a five-line CI tail shows
   nothing whatsoever. The rules are written into the new file's own comments; consider
   whether they belong in `CLAUDE.md` where the next person writing a widget test will see
   them.

**For Michael**
1. **Nothing — this is complete.** Committed on `main`; push when you like.
2. Nothing in the app looks or behaves differently. No user-visible copy changed, so the
   website drift check is unaffected.
3. **What you are getting for it:** the four screens you had to find by hand on a phone —
   "Offline", "N records aren't on the server", "N records the server sent could not be
   read", and "You're no longer on this project" — will now fail the build if somebody breaks
   them, instead of being found on a hillside.

**Resolved 2026-09-02 by the planning session.**
1. **Confirmed. Nothing above the line remains** — this was the last of it.
2. **Written into `/w-10`, in the words you used, plus the thing that makes it not merely a
   note.** The override to reach for is `serverTransportProvider`;
   `membershipTransportProvider` still works and still covers membership only. **And the
   header table in `sync_bar_states_end_to_end_test.dart` is what decides what is
   photographable** — three of the fourteen are facts about a clock or about an address
   refused before a connection exists, so a content task guessing from the screen would shoot
   at states no substituted server can produce.
3. **Also `/w-10`, and the correction is bigger than the comment.** `joined.dart`'s claim that
   the sync engine is never faked **is true of a `membershipTransportProvider` capture and
   false of a `serverTransportProvider` one.** So the task is told to make each capture say
   which override it uses, rather than just fixing the stale mechanism — otherwise the file
   ends up carrying a sentence that is true of some of its captures and false of others,
   which is worse than what it has now.
4. **You added it to `CLAUDE.md` yourself and it is right, so it stays** — the boundary point
   is minor and worth one sentence: **you asked the planning session to consider it and then
   wrote it in the same commit.** For a rule the next person writing a widget test will
   read, that is the better outcome; the reason to keep asking is that `CLAUDE.md` is where
   the two sessions' shared rules live, and a rule added by one session that the other has
   not seen is how the file stops being shared. **No change; noted so the habit stays
   deliberate.**

**One thing this task did that is worth recording separately, because it is the finding and
the report almost buried it under the deliverable.** Every one of the eleven tests was first
run against the old code. **Nine failed, and all nine failed identically — the bar said
"Offline".** With the engine building its own connection, substituting a server did not give
you a *failing* server, it gave you *no* server, so the only two states any test could reach
were the two describing a request that never arrived. **That is a check that could not
distinguish success from its own failure, at the level of an entire test surface rather than
one assertion** — and it is the reason no state, once reachable, turned out to be wrong: they
had never been wrong, they had been unreachable. **A seam is not a convenience; it is what
makes a negative result mean anything.**

   (`test/data/sync/refused_name_is_not_a_loop_test.dart`). **The caveat 11.89

   five times.** All five are now fixed in `PERMISSIONS_MATRIX.md`, and §4.2 carries

   than the fixes: **two different operations were both numbered M9** (re-admission,
   added by 11.81, and the device-sessions row, from 11.35) — re-admission is now

   laptop, let alone a server. **And `ensureServerAppRole`'s own comment already said a purge
   would need its own narrower credential.** The knowledge was in the file. Nobody read it back,
   **because nothing ran it.** A `tritrack_retention` role with read-and-delete on three tables,
   no login, **watched failing first with a real `permission denied`** — that is the right shape.
2. **Task 11.119, and your framing is what makes it worth doing rather than another sweep.**
   *"The common factor is not the code — it is that the falsified thing was never run."* **The
   question is not whether a control is correct but whether it has ever been executed**, and you
   are right that this is a different search from the ones already done. **It is written to be
   different on purpose:** 11.88 answered this for gate instruments and found two; this asks it
   of the app and the server, and is told that **if the method reduces to re-running 11.88's,
   the scope is wrong.** It must include what coverage tools structurally cannot see — scheduled
   jobs, CLI entrypoints, healthchecks — **because the purge was a program nothing called, and no
   coverage report would have flagged it.** And it is a survey: **forbidden from fixing what it
   finds**, because fixing instances inside a survey is how a survey stops halfway.
3, 4. **Closed and recorded.**
5. **Ratified, and the reasoning is the deciding part, not the number.** A check red for part of
   every day teaches people to ignore it, **which is task 10.12's argument and the same one that
   justified the dismiss on the stale sync bar.** 48 hours stands unless Michael says otherwise;
   it is one line in `.env` and the reasoning is written where he can argue with it.
6. **Noted, and it is a small example of the same class this task is about.** A reader that
   absorbed the *next* service's comment block **turned a passing test red for a property that
   was still true** — a check reporting a fault in something correct is the mirror image of one
   reporting health in something broken, and both are the instrument lying.
7. **Confirmed: 11.80 is unaffected and Michael can start it.**

**And his risk is carried to him plainly: the first sweep permanently deletes rows on his
existing server.** That is the task working as designed, and it is still worth him knowing before
`docker compose up` rather than after.
