### Task 11.116 — 2026-09-01 — commit 6164a39 — Done

**For the planning session**

1. **Nothing is blocked, but one decision is now written down and worth knowing about.**
   When the app comes back holding a failure it has not re-tested, it **shows the failure and
   says it has not re-tested it** — same colour, same icon, same urgency, plus the clause
   "Last tried 3 days ago — not retried since." The reasoning is in the class note on
   `RememberedSyncFailure` (`lib/data/sync/remembered_sync_failure.dart`) and summarised in
   the plan entry. If a future task wants to soften a remembered failure's colour, that
   contradicts this decision on purpose — the note says why.
2. **The staleness question 11.114 raised is answered and needs no task.** The 24-hour clock
   runs from the last *successful* round (`lastSuccessAt`, written only after a round that
   connected), not from the last attempt. A device that keeps trying and keeps failing does
   **not** look fresh. Nothing to fix.
3. **Ask the planning session to note one thing found while in there, already fixed in this
   commit, in case the class recurs:** changing the sync frequency rebuilt the status and
   dropped the failure fields, so tapping that control reset the bar to healthy with no
   restart involved. That is the same class as this task — a state that only exists in memory
   being thrown away by an unrelated rebuild — and it is the second instance of it on this
   provider. **A sweep for other providers that rebuild a status object field-by-field and
   silently drop a field would be a reasonable task**, because the pattern here is a
   constructor call listing fifteen fields by hand, in seven places, with no compiler help if
   one is left out. That sweep is not in the plan and I have not done it.

**For Michael**

1. **Nothing to run or decide.** Committed as `6164a39` on `main`; push when you next push.
2. **What changed for you:** if sync has been failing and you close and reopen the app, the
   bar no longer goes calm. It keeps saying what is wrong, and adds that the app has not tried
   again since. Once it does try — which happens on the next foreground — the clause goes away
   and you are back to a live answer.
3. **One risk you are now carrying, and it is small:** the app can now show a failure the
   server may have recovered from. That window is normally seconds, because a restart still
   triggers an attempt. It stays open indefinitely only if you have sync set to
   "Only when I ask" — and in that case the clause on the bar is exactly the thing telling you
   so.

**Resolved 2026-09-01 by the planning session.**

1. **The decision is right and is now recorded in the plan as well as the class note**, so a
   future task cannot soften it by accident. **Showing the failure at full strength and saying
   the app has not re-tested it** is the honest reading: **the failure's severity has not
   changed — only the app's confidence about *now* has** — and that belongs in a clause rather
   than in a colour. Putting the reasoning where somebody would meet it before changing it is
   what makes the decision durable rather than a preference.
2. **Answered, and it is the answer that keeps 11.114 honest.** The 24-hour clock runs from
   `lastSuccessAt` — written only after a round that connected — so **a device that keeps
   trying and keeps failing does not look fresh.** Had it run from the last attempt, the
   warning 11.114 built would never have fired on the case it exists for. **No task, and the
   question is closed rather than left as a doubt.**
3. **Task 11.117, and the framing you gave it is what makes it worth doing.** *"A constructor
   call listing fifteen fields by hand, in seven places, with no compiler help if one is left
   out"* — **that is the hand-maintained-list class wearing a constructor**, and it is this
   project's oldest defect in its third costume. **Two instances, both user-visible, both on
   the app's most important indicator, and the only feedback either gave was a bar that looked
   calm.**

   **The task is written as removing the invitation rather than finding the instances**: prefer
   `copyWith` or whatever makes *"everything as before, except this"* the only easy way to
   write a rebuild, **because if a rebuild cannot omit a field, the next instance cannot
   happen** and no future sweep is needed. The sweep follows, with the count and the rejected
   candidates.

   **And one thing about how you found the second instance is written into it: by accident,
   while doing something else.** Nothing was watching that path — so it gets a test, not
   because it is broken now, but because it was invisible until somebody happened to look.

**Your risk note is the right shape and goes to Michael as written**: the app can now show a
failure the server may have recovered from, the window is normally seconds because a restart
still triggers an attempt, **and it stays open indefinitely only under "Only when I ask" — in
which case the clause on the bar is exactly the thing telling him so.** A residual that
announces itself is not the same kind of residual.

### Task 11.114 — 2026-09-01 — commit `9ebfea8` (plan-doc hash fixed up in `0537e42`) — Done
**For the planning session**
1. Point 6 of the design (Phase 11 Discovered Scope, "the stale sync bar") asked to
   either fold in the restart-amnesia bug or say why not. I did not fold it in — it
   needs `SyncFailureCause` and `SyncSchedule`'s `consecutiveFailures`/`stoppedReason`
   persisted durably per project, which `SyncController.build` does not do today (it
   only persists `frequency` and `lastAttemptAt`), so a genuine ongoing failure still
   resets to a calm "healthy" bar on every app restart or provider rebuild, not only
   in the >24h case this task closes. Please open a new task number for that
   persistence work; I wrote the reasoning inline in the Discovered Scope entry so it
   doesn't need re-deriving.
2. Task 11.115 ("no signal vs. server off") is unaffected by this task and still
   waiting, as before.
**For Michael**
1. Nothing — this is complete and safe to use as-is.

*No further entries. Task 11.113's two entries were resolved 2026-09-01.*

**Resolved 2026-09-01 by the planning session.**

1. **Task 11.116, beta-blocking — and declining to fold it in was right.** It needs durable
   per-project state that does not exist, and folding an unbuilt persistence layer into a
   presentation task is how a bounded task becomes an open one. **Writing the reasoning inline
   in the Discovered Scope entry so it does not need re-deriving is what made the hand-off
   free.**

   **The finding is broader than the entry's own framing suggests, and 11.116 says so: the
   bar's memory is shorter than the failure it reports.** A restart is not rare — **a phone
   reclaiming a backgrounded app is one, and a provider rebuild does not even need the app to
   close** — so a device whose sync has been refused for a week can show a calm bar several
   times a day. **11.114 bounds that to a day rather than fixing it**, which is the right
   description of what this task achieved and is now recorded as such.

   **Two things added to 11.116 beyond the persistence work.** The decision it must make out
   loud: **is a remembered failure still true?** Showing it as current is a claim the app has
   not re-tested; discarding it is the defect; **the honest middle distinguishes *this is
   failing* from *this was failing when we last tried and we have not tried since*** — a real
   difference to somebody deciding whether to walk half a mile for signal. And a check that
   could be this same defect wearing 11.114's clothes: **`lastAttemptAt` is persisted, so
   establish whether the staleness clock runs from last attempt or last success.** If it runs
   from attempt, a device that keeps trying and keeps failing looks fresh forever, **and the
   warning this task just built would never fire on the case it exists for.**
2. **Noted; 11.115 is unchanged and still below the line.**

### Task 11.113 — 2026-09-01 — commit `191bc6e` — Done

**What changed, in one sentence.** The app used to decide "why did that request fail?"
in two different places, so a server with a self-signed certificate was named correctly
on the Server Connection screen and reported as **"Offline"** on the sync bar at the same
moment; there is now one place that decides, both surfaces read it, and a test goes red
if a third place appears.

**For the planning session**

1. **Please ask Michael to re-run the original report on his iPhone before this is called
   closed.** I could not test iOS at all — it needs a physical device. The macOS half was
   run by hand on this machine and passes, and macOS uses the same code path (`NSURLSession`
   through `CupertinoClient`), so I have reasonable but not complete confidence. **What he
   should see:** a red bar reading "Not a network problem — this device doesn't trust the
   server's security certificate", never "Offline".
2. **A separate finding, not fixed here, and it deserves a task number: the sync bar's
   colour never changes just because sync has stopped happening.** The bar shows "Synced 21
   hr ago" in the same calm grey it shows "Synced 2 min ago". Only a *failed attempt*
   changes it, and after a restart the app forgets the last failure and goes back to calm
   until something tries again. **A field tech whose sync broke on Monday sees a calm bar
   all week** and finds out on Friday. This is why Michael saw a calm bar against a server
   the app had never contacted. **Ask for a task: decide at what age "Synced N ago" stops
   being reassuring and starts being a warning.** I did not guess at a threshold — that is
   a judgement about how these crews work, not about code.
3. **A second separate finding, same shape, smaller: "my phone has no signal" and "the
   server is switched off" are one state in this app**, both reported as "Offline". Nothing
   on the wire tells them apart, so distinguishing them needs a device-connectivity check
   the app does not currently have. **This is the same class this task exists to close** —
   a cause named wrongly sends somebody to the wrong place — so it is worth a task rather
   than a note, but it is a genuinely harder one and I am not recommending it be urgent.
4. **The rule this task's check enforces, for reuse:** *only one file under `lib/` may name
   a transport exception type.* It lives in
   `test/documentation/one_transport_classifier_test.dart` and it is the same shape as task
   11.98's checked vocabulary. **What it would have caught:** task 11.108, the moment the
   second classifier was written — and the sync bar would then have inherited certificates
   without anybody thinking about sync. **What it would not have caught:** the original
   absence (no check catches "nobody thought of TLS"), or a surface that classified on a
   status code or on message text instead of on a type. Both limits are written into the
   test file itself.
5. **One judgement call to record.** The task said to rank a rejected certificate where the
   `http://` refusal sits. I also made it reach the bar on the **first** failed round rather
   than the third, unlike "offline" — a certificate is refused identically every time, so
   waiting for three attempts only means saying something false twice first. If that was not
   intended, it is one line in `sync_provider.dart`.

**For Michael**

### Task 11.108 — 2026-09-01 — commit 4a29b4a — Done
**For the planning session**
1. Add a task number for the Discovered Scope entry this task filed (2026-09-01, in Phase 11's
   Discovered Scope, right before the Backlog heading): the same wrong-cause defect this task
   fixed — an untrusted certificate reported as "this device could not tell why," or here as
   "could not reach the server" — is still live on iOS and macOS. This app uses a different HTTP
   client on those two platforms (`CupertinoClient`), and its TLS failures arrive as a plain
   `http.ClientException` rather than `HandshakeException`, so they're still caught by the
   existing "could not reach the server" branch instead of getting a certificate-specific
   message. I found this reading `cupertino_http`'s source, not by testing on a device — see
   the entry for what a fix would look like (it can use `NSURLErrorDomain` codes, which are more
   reliable than the free-text string this task had to fall back to on the other platforms).
**For Michael**
1. Nothing to run. Git is committed (`4a29b4a`) and the working tree is clean.
2. If you test this on an iPhone or a Mac against a server with a self-signed or expired
   certificate, expect it to still say "Could not reach the server" rather than naming the
   certificate — that's the gap above, not a new bug.

**Resolved 2026-09-01 by the planning session. Task 11.112, beta-blocking.**

**The finding is more consequential than its one paragraph suggests, and the entry should say
so: this defect is now fixed on the platforms nobody is testing on, and still live on the two
Michael uses.** `CupertinoClient` on iOS and macOS delivers TLS failures as a plain
`http.ClientException` rather than `HandshakeException`, so they still fall to *"could not reach
the server"*. **From his chair, nothing changed.**

**That is not a criticism of the task.** It fixed what its brief named, and **it disclosed the
gap instead of letting a green suite speak for it** — which is the only reason anybody knows.
The brief said *"do not just add a `HandshakeException` case"* and the reason it gave was that
two exceptions in two days had reached one catch-all; **the answer turned out to be that a third
route reaches it on a different client**, which is a better finding than the one the brief
anticipated.

**And you were right to say you found it by reading `cupertino_http`'s source rather than by
testing.** 11.112 carries that as a hypothesis to confirm rather than a measurement to act on —
**macOS it can test itself; iOS needs Michael and a phone** — and it must say what was verified
where.

**One thing added on top of your write-up, from your own observation that `NSURLErrorDomain`
codes are more reliable than the free text you had to fall back to.** That fallback is **a
control that works for a reason nobody controls**: a Dart or OS update changes the message, the
branch silently stops matching, and the app quietly returns to reporting the wrong cause **with
every test still green.** So 11.112 must **use the structured codes on Apple platforms and leave
a test that fails if your matched string ever changes** — and it is told not to unify the two
behind one free-text matcher for tidiness, because a code and a string are different qualities
of evidence.

### Task 11.107 — 2026-08-31 — commit `402d8ba` — Done

**The 38.2-second wait became 1.6 seconds, and the splash screen can now say it failed.**

**The decision, since the brief said this was one and not a defect fix: keep automatic retry,
bound it, and hand the person the retry.** `lib/core/providers/retry_policy.dart` is the whole
policy and the whole reasoning — three attempts, 400 ms then 1200 ms of backoff, then the error
is delivered. It is installed on `main.dart`'s `ProviderScope`, which is every provider in the
running app, and on the container the full-app widget tests boot so a test measures what ships.

**What gets worse, named as the brief required.** Retries exist because a field connection drops
and comes back, so switching them off was not on the table. But an outage lasting between two and
thirty-eight seconds used to be ridden out invisibly and now surfaces as a failure somebody has to
tap past. That is the right way round: a person who sees what happened after 1.6 seconds and can
press a button is better served than one shown nothing for 38 and unable to tell the app from a
freeze. **Automatic retry was also never this app's network resilience** — a failed sync is
retried by `SyncController.syncIfDue` on every foreground and by the Sync Status screen, neither
of which this touches.

**What a person sees during the wait.** On the splash, the "WILDLIFE TELEMETRY" tagline slot is
replaced by a spinner and "Still trying…" the moment an attempt has failed and another is
scheduled — read from Riverpod's own `AsyncValue.retrying`, so it reflects a real retry rather
than a timer guessing at one.

**The splash screen's second half.** It had no `try`: a failed identity read left the error
unhandled, `context.go` never ran, and the first screen anybody ever sees stayed on brand green
forever with nothing said. It now catches, shows a panel headed "TriTrack could not finish
starting up" with plain sentences and a next step, and offers a "Try again" that invalidates the
provider and really re-reads. **Nothing of the caught exception reaches the screen** — on this
screen it would be a Riverpod or sqflite sentence. Where the error is Riverpod's stand-in for one
it destroyed, the panel says "This device could not tell why" rather than inventing a cause.

**The test was confirmed red beforehand, and red for the right reason.** The first run failed to
compile, which is not evidence, so the three string constants were added to the screen with no
behaviour change and the run repeated: all three tests failed on the frozen splash. There are now
four, including one that presses "Try again" and asserts the app actually leaves the splash.
`test/documentation/retry_policy_applied_test.dart` fails if a `ProviderScope` is ever added
without a retry policy. 1723 app tests pass; `flutter analyze` is clean.

**For the planning session**

1. **One thing this task deliberately did not do, and it may deserve a task.** The policy makes
   every awaited provider on every screen fail within 1.6 seconds instead of 38. **It does not
   check that each of those roughly thirty call sites renders anything when it does.** I read the
   list and they are almost all inside a `try`, but "inside a try" is not "shows the person
   something" — that is exactly the distinction task 11.105's follow-up found sixty instances of.
   **Ask for a task to walk the awaited-provider call sites and confirm each one has a visible
   failure state**, or say in writing that the bounded wait is enough on its own. I am flagging
   this as uncertainty, not as a known defect: I did not find a specific screen that goes blank.
2. **The 400/1200 ms numbers are mine, not Michael's.** They are argued in `retry_policy.dart`
   and pinned by a test, so changing them is one line plus a reason. If the planning session
   wants a different budget, it is cheap to change; nothing else depends on the values.
3. **Nothing else.** No plan re-scope, no new dependency, no discovered scope.

**For Michael**

1. **Committed as `402d8ba`. Push when you like.** Nothing is staged that this task did not edit.
2. **One thing only you can run, and it is worth running.** On a phone, put the device in
   airplane mode and open TriTrack, then use it — the app should now admit a failure in under two
   seconds rather than sitting still. **The splash failure itself is hard to reach on purpose**
   (it needs the device's local user row to be unreadable), so I could not reproduce it on
   hardware; it is covered by tests only, and I am telling you that rather than implying I saw it.
3. **A decision you may want to make, but do not have to.** 1.6 seconds is my choice of how long
   the app tries before it admits a problem. If, in the field, you find yourself tapping "try
   again" on things that then work, the number is too low and it is a one-line change. Say so and
   it moves.
4. **A risk you are now carrying, and it is smaller than the one it replaces.** A network blip
   lasting between two and thirty-eight seconds used to heal invisibly and will now show you an
   error you have to dismiss. That is the price of never being shown a frozen-looking app, and I
   think it is the right trade, but it is a real change in what a bad-signal day feels like.

---

**Resolved 2026-08-31 by the planning session. Michael ran the airplane-mode check and it
passed: app started in airplane mode, no freezing behaviour.**

**The decision is ratified and the numbers stand.** Keep automatic retry, bound it, hand the
person the retry — and **naming what gets worse** is what makes it a decision rather than a
preference: an outage between two and thirty-eight seconds used to be ridden out invisibly and
now surfaces as something to tap past. **That is the right way round**, and your reason is the
one to keep: automatic retry was never this app's network resilience — `syncIfDue` on every
foreground and the Sync Status screen are, and neither was touched.

**400 ms and 1200 ms are accepted as yours.** They are argued in the file and pinned by a test,
which is the condition under which a session's own numbers should stand. **No change wanted.**

**Reading `AsyncValue.retrying` rather than running a timer beside it is the detail worth
naming.** A spinner driven by a timer would say "still trying" whether or not anything was —
**a control that cannot distinguish its subject from its own clock**, which is this project's
oldest defect in a new costume. You used the real signal.

**And the red-test discipline held under a case that usually defeats it.** The first run failed
to **compile**, you said out loud that this is not evidence, added the three string constants
with no behaviour change, and repeated it. **A test that fails because the code does not build
has told you nothing**, and most people count it.

### Task 11.105 follow-up — 2026-08-31 — commit 41ba510 — Done

**Michael asked for this directly and chose its scope.** Task 11.105's report flagged that a
failed CSV import shows a raw database error, and suggested a checked rule for the class. He
asked what that meant, then said yes. **I had told him it was three instances. It was sixty**
— reported back before doing any work, with the scope choice put to him; he chose to fix all
forty-six user-visible ones rather than grandfather any onto an allowlist.

**The count.** 60 sites interpolate a caught exception into a string. 10 are `debugPrint`
behind `kDebugMode` — developer logs, correctly left. 4 chain a cause into a new exception in
the data layer — not display. **46 put a raw error on a screen**, and all 46 are fixed.

**What was built.** `describeFailure` (`lib/core/errors/failure_message.dart`) is now the one
place deciding what a person is told; it shows an exception's own text only for types whose
message was written for a person, against a stated three-point bar. **Most of this app's own
exception types fail it** — `UnauthorizedMutation`, `LastOwnerRemoval`, `NotAProjectMember`
and `PublishNotYoursToMake` all end in a raw UUID — so the list has one entry and everything
else gets a sentence written at the call site. `LoadFailure` covers the 29 `.when(error:)`
branches, which were one situation rather than 29 judgements.
`test/documentation/raw_error_in_ui_test.dart` is the standing check.

**Two things found during the work are worth more than the sweep itself.**

- **The check was blind.** A fixed 600-character window on arrow bodies meant a `Text` in
  `server_config_screen.dart` had its `$e` past the window, and the check reported *all
  clear* on a file that still had the defect in it. **It was only caught because a subagent
  reported a site it had deliberately left behind** — not by the check, and not by me. It now
  balances brackets, and both shapes are verified red against a deliberately reintroduced
  defect.
- **Task 11.105's own guard rejected new code written for this commit.** An `InvalidServerUrl`
  extractor was added to the authored-message list, on the reasoning that its message is
  exactly the right kind — and it was dead, because `requireValidServerUrl` is called only
  from an autoDispose provider's build. Written by somebody who had just spent a day on that
  exact defect and reintroduced it anyway. Kept in the file as a comment rather than silently
  dropped.

**One correction to subagent work, flagged because it is the recurring class.** A written
message promised *"your project is exactly as it was"* after a failed backup import. The
comment two lines above it says §4.19's consent rule makes the import two-phase and the first
pass may write whatever destroys nothing — so a second-phase failure leaves those additions
committed. **Copy describing a mechanism the code does not have, which is the defect task
11.54 exists to catch.** Corrected to say what is true, and that re-importing is safe.

**For the planning session**

1. **Two more findings need task numbers** (both written into Phase 11's Discovered Scope):
   - **A viewshed that fails tells nobody anything.** `ComputationFailed` is referenced only
     in the file that declares it; the map's progress bar renders only the *running* case, so
     on failure the bar vanishes and the person is told nothing. The sweep wrote a real
     sentence into that state because it is what a renderer would use — **nothing draws it.**
   - **The viewshed has no control its failure message can point at.** The 10 km range is
     hard-coded, so "try a smaller radius" describes a control that does not exist. The
     shipped wording works around it; decide whether a range control is worth having.
2. **The four findings in the 11.105 entry below still need task numbers** — nothing here
   changed them. The 38-second retry is still the one I would number first.
3. **`server_identity_adopter.dart:347` interpolates a list of column names into a
   user-visible refusal reason.** Not an exception dump and it carries no user data, so the

### Task 11.105 — 2026-08-31 — commit 9939b1f — Done

**The headline, because it changes what the task was:** the brief's mechanism was wrong, and
that is the most useful thing found. Riverpod 3.3.2 does **not** wrap a provider's error in
`ProviderException` at `await ref.read(p.future)` — measured, the raw exception arrives
intact, for every provider shape and through chains of them. What kills a typed `catch` is
**autoDispose teardown**: the element is disposed while still loading and the caller gets a
`StateError` about that, so **the original is destroyed rather than wrapped** and no unwrap at
the `catch` could ever recover it. The re-briefing note task 11.104 left in Phase 12's
Discovered Scope was right, and it is now the whole story rather than half of it.

**The count.** 33 `try` blocks in `lib/` type-test an exception; 44 (site, type) pairs; five
sit around an awaited provider. **One was dead** — the location-denied branch in Project
Setup. The other 43 were traced individually to a reachable throw site and are live. **None
was dead for the second reason the brief asked about** (a type that can no longer be thrown),
so nothing had to be removed. 11.66's other instance, the refused `http://` address, was the
same mechanism but not a dead catch — nothing caught `InvalidServerUrl` and nothing could.
**So the answer is the one the brief said would be a real result: 11.66 found all of them.**

**For the planning session**

1. **Four findings need task numbers.** All four are written up in Phase 11's Discovered
   Scope with the file and line; these are the one-line versions.
   - **A failed provider makes the app wait 38 seconds before it can say anything.** Riverpod
     3 retries automatically — ten attempts, backoff to a 6.4s ceiling, measured at 38.2
     seconds — and `p.future` stays pending throughout. Nothing sets `retry:` on the app's
     `ProviderScope`, so this is every awaited provider on every screen. **This is a decision,
     not a defect fix:** either the app sets its own retry policy, or each awaiting call site
     gets a timeout. Task 11.105 bounded only the site it touched, using a timeout that was
     already there.
   - **An untrusted TLS certificate on the LAN server reports "this device could not tell
     why".** `HandshakeException` is neither `SocketException` nor `http.ClientException`, so
     it falls to the catch-all in `server_config_screen.dart`. **This is the beta path, not an
     edge case** — 10.49 committed a terminating proxy and §4.1 requires https, so an
     untrusted certificate is the first thing a tester meets. Same wrong-cause class as 11.104.
   - **A failed identity read leaves the app on the splash screen forever, with no message.**
     `splash_screen.dart:59-63` has no `try`; the error goes unhandled and `context.go` never
     runs. Combined with the retry above, the app looks frozen for 38 seconds and then stays
     frozen.
   - **A failed CSV tag import shows a raw database error, SQL and bound values included.**
     `tag_database_screen.dart:335`. **This is task 11.46's defect, still live in the second of
     its two places** — 11.46 removed exactly this interpolation from the publish path and left
     a 20-line comment saying why it must never return, and nobody swept for the other one.
     Worth deciding whether "no user-visible string interpolates a caught exception" becomes a
     checked rule; this is its third instance.
2. **Task 11.106's back-gesture item now has a neighbour worth grouping with it, or not** —
   your call. Nothing in 11.105 touched it; flagging only because item 3 above is also a
   "the app appears to have stopped" defect and they may read better as one task.
3. **No re-scope needed for anything already written.** 11.104's re-briefing note in Phase 12's
   Discovered Scope can be marked resolved: both mechanisms it asked for are covered, and the
   `ProviderException` half turned out not to occur at this seam at all.

**For Michael**

1. **Nothing to run and nothing to decide.** Committed as `9939b1f`; push when you like.
2. **One thing you may notice on a phone:** with location denied, Project Setup's "Use current
   location" now names the actual reason instead of telling you to go outdoors. If you can,
   try it in all three states — permission denied once, permission denied permanently, and
   location switched off for the whole device — because those are three different sentences
   and only the middle one is easy to reach by accident.
3. **A risk you are still carrying, unchanged by this task:** the 38-second retry above is
   live on every screen. Nothing is broken by it, but any failure anywhere in the app looks
   like a freeze for most of a minute first. It needs a task.

### Task 11.104 — 2026-08-31 — commit 270964d — Done

**For the planning session**

1. **Re-brief task 11.105 before it is run. Its stated mechanism is wrong for the
   instance it was written from.** 11.105's entry says Riverpod 3 wraps a provider's
   error in `ProviderException`, so a typed `catch` at an awaited provider can never
   match. I measured it against the real providers on 2026-08-31, and at this site
   that is not what happens: `await ref.read(serverHttpClientProvider.future)` — the
   exact call `SyncController._engine` and `CurrentSession._requireClient` make —
   returns neither a `ProviderException` nor the original `InvalidServerUrl`. It
   returns `StateError: "The provider serverHttpClientProvider was disposed during
   loading state, yet no value could be emitted."` The provider is autoDispose and
   `ref.read(...future)` holds no listener across the await, so the element is torn
   down while its body is still running and **the original error is destroyed rather
   than wrapped.** A shared unwrap of `ProviderException` would fix nothing here.
   **Ask for 11.105 to cover both mechanisms**, and to say plainly that for the
   second one a better `catch` is not the fix — reading the condition as a value from
   a provider that cannot throw is, which is what this task did.
2. **The count in the report 11.105 is asked for will be wrong if it counts catch
   sites.** Two of the four sites that read the http client used `ref.read`
   (the autoDispose mechanism) and one used `ref.watch` (which may be the
   `ProviderException` mechanism — I did not manage to reproduce the watch case
   cleanly and am not claiming it). **I am uncertain which mechanism applies to any
   given site without measuring it**, and that uncertainty is itself the finding: the
   sweep has to measure each one, not classify it by reading the code.
3. **Four things fixed here that were not in the brief, all recorded in Phase 11's
   Discovered Scope**, and none of them needs a task — they are done. Listed so the
   plan is not surprised by them: the URL field's placeholder proposed the exact
   address a release build refuses; the validator used `Uri.isAbsolute`, which is
   false whenever a fragment is present, so it rejected an address `ServerConfig`
   would have accepted; a security test asserted a typed-in count of two occurrences
   and went red when one function became two, with no control changed; and the
   refusal check now also runs at the publish, join and membership seams, not only
   the sync one.
4. **User-visible copy changed**, per the content-stream rule. The Server URL field's
   error messages (one sentence became five), the Server Connection header when an
   address is refused, the sync bar and the sync-status screen's headline for that
   state. **I checked `website/` and none of these strings is quoted there**, so the
   drift check should stay green — but the content lane may want the new refused-
   address state in the guide, because it is the state a beta tester on `README.md`
   §4's procedure lands in.
5. **Not done, and deliberately: `README.md` §4 still ends in an `http://` address.**
   The app now explains the refusal properly, so the documented path no longer
   produces a false cause. Whether §4 should additionally tell a beta tester to run a
   debug build, or whether the LAN prototype needs TLS before the beta, is a decision
   about the beta's shape rather than about this screen — **11.66 raised it and it is

**For Michael**

1. **Nothing to push unless you want to** — committed as `270964d` on `main`. Push

2. **Please re-run the Android walkthrough's server step on a real release build.**

4. **A risk you are now carrying, and it is smaller than it was.** I fixed the four

**Resolved 2026-08-31 by the planning session — all three entries.**

**First, the correction, because it is mine.** **The brief's mechanism was wrong.** I wrote
that Riverpod 3 wraps a provider's error in `ProviderException` at `await .future`, and it
does not — measured at 3.3.2, for every provider shape and through chains. **What kills a
typed catch is autoDispose teardown: the element is disposed while still loading, the caller
gets a `StateError` about that, and the original is destroyed rather than wrapped**, so no
unwrap at the `catch` could ever have recovered it. **The task measured the hypothesis instead
of implementing it**, which is the only reason the fix is not a shared unwrap that would have
done nothing.

**And the answer to the question the brief said would be a real result is the one it named:
11.66 found all of them.** One dead catch out of 44 pairs, and none dead for the second reason
asked about. **A count of one, reported as a count of one**, is what closing a class looks
like.

**Michael's sixty.** The follow-up was told three instances and found sixty; **it reported
that back before doing any work and put the scope choice to him**, and he chose to fix all
forty-six user-visible ones rather than grandfather any. **Reporting a tenfold estimate error
before spending the budget is the behaviour that makes an estimate worth giving.**

**Two things in that entry are worth more than the sweep, and both are the same shape.**
**The check was blind** — a fixed 600-character window meant it reported *all clear* on a file
that still contained the defect, and **it was caught only because a subagent reported a site
it had deliberately left behind**, not by the check and not by the task. And **the guard
rejected new code written for this very commit**: an `InvalidServerUrl` extractor added on
sound reasoning, dead because `requireValidServerUrl` is called only from an autoDispose
build — **written by somebody who had just spent a day on that exact defect and reintroduced
it anyway.** Keeping it as a comment rather than silently dropping it is the right record.

**The findings, all numbered:**

- **The 38-second retry and the forever splash screen are one task, 11.107, beta-blocking.**
  They compose: the retry makes the splash-screen hang look like a slow freeze before it
  becomes a permanent one, on the first screen anybody sees. **You were right that the retry
  is a decision rather than a defect fix**, and 11.107 is told the number is not the problem —
  the silence is.
- **The untrusted certificate is task 11.108, beta-blocking**, and it is told **not** to just
  add a `HandshakeException` branch. **Two exceptions in two days reaching the same catch-all
  is a signal about the catch-all**, so it must enumerate what else arrives there.
- **The CSV import raw error is closed by your own follow-up** — all 46 sites, with a standing
  check.
- **Both viewshed findings fold into task 11.87**, which is now the viewshed task rather than
  the viewshed-boundary task. **A message nobody can reach is not a message**, and a message
  pointing at a control that does not exist is the inverse of the class this project keeps
  finding.
- **`server_identity_adopter.dart:347` goes to task 11.58**, which is the next thing that will
  touch server identity. Your judgement was right: not an exception dump, no user data, but
  technical wording a person reads — a line in a task rather than a task.

**Your grouping question, answered: keep 11.106 and 11.107 separate.** 11.106 is Android
platform convention; 11.107 is the app-appears-stopped class on every platform. **They read as
neighbours and they are not the same failure**, and merging them would put a beta-blocker
behind a batch of visual polish.

**And the correction to subagent work is the one to keep repeating.** *"Your project is
exactly as it was"* after a failed backup import, when §4.19's two-phase consent rule means
the first pass may already have written whatever destroys nothing. **Copy describing a
mechanism the code does not have — caught in review rather than in the field, which is the
first time that has happened rather than the other way round.**

### Task 11.95 — 2026-08-31 — commits 21d4c61 (item 2) and 2a58ac5 (item 1) — Done

**The unknown is answered, and the answer is that there is no second fault.** `/w-02` saw
Riverpod refuse a provider write during the map's build, and then, seconds later, an
unhandled asynchronous error it could not account for. **They are one error.**
`_computeViewshedAt` is `async`, and the provider write Riverpod refuses sat *outside* that
function's own `try` — so the refusal never became a caught failure. It completed an
un-awaited future with an error nobody was listening to, which is why the same single error
surfaced twice by two routes. Measured rather than deduced: the stack runs
`Future._asyncCompleteError` → `_maybeAutoComputeViewshed` → `_buildBody`, and pumping the
real map screen with a GPS fix produced **exactly one** non-tile-fetch error before the
change and **none** after.

**What the release build kept while hiding the message.** Throwing past the `try` also
jumped the `finally`, so the automatic viewshed never ran and the bottom progress bar sat at
"Computing viewshed…" for the rest of the session. A field tech got no message, no viewshed,
and a progress bar that never finished. Both halves are now asserted by a test, and both
assertions were confirmed red against the old code.

**Both flagged phone screenshots regenerate clean, and I looked at the pixels.** The map's
credit is now two readable lines ending in "(CC-BY-SA)", clear of the "+" button, with no
overflow stripes; the position screen's fits on one line. Nothing was written into
`website/` — the run was the compare-only form, which stages into `build/screenshots/`.

   the field prefilled from the phone's GPS accuracy at 4 m, deleting the 4 to type 10 put
   the 4 straight back on the next frame. The only way to enter 10 was to type `410` and
   then delete the leading digit. **The cause is this project's standing defect class,
   again:** an empty field and a never-touched field are different states, both of them
   read as `truthPrecisionM == null`, and the prefill treated a deliberate clear as an
   empty slot to fill. Fixed by recording the fact (`truthPrecisionTouched`) rather than
   inferring it from a value with two meanings, and by replacing `setTruthPrecision`'s
   boolean with three methods that each name who acted — `prefillTruthPrecision` (the
   app), `enterTruthPrecision` (the person), `withdrawTruthPrecisionPrefill` (the app
   taking its own guess back). **The regression test was confirmed to fail against the old
   logic**, reproducing Michael's `4` exactly, before being kept.
   - **Worth a look during the next sweep:** this is the second time in two days that a
     null with two meanings has been the whole defect. If there is a cheap way to find the
     rest of that class — prefilled fields whose "has the user touched this" test is the
     value itself — it would be worth a task. **I did not sweep for it here**, so I do not
     know how many there are.

### Task 11.91 — 2026-08-31 — commit 0c77ce4 — Done
**For the planning session**
1. Nothing.

**For Michael**
1. Nothing — this is complete. Nothing to run, no decision needed, and the repo is
   committed and clean.

For context: this closed the bug task 11.88 found — two different security checks in
`scripts/verify_11_49_server_reads.py` that happened to have the same written
description, where the second one silently erased the first one's result instead of
being reported. That is why one of the tool's self-tests (deliberately breaking the
server to prove the tool would notice) had been reporting "did not notice" for two
checks that had, in fact, noticed — the tool's own bookkeeping was throwing the answer
away, not the server hiding anything.

The fix makes a reused description a hard error the moment it happens, naming both
places it was used, so this can't happen silently again. Five actual collisions were
found this way (one three-way, more than the four originally suspected) and are now
each written with the route name attached so they can't collide again; one suspected
collision turned out, on inspection, not to be a real one and was left alone. I then
re-ran the full check — both the plain pass and the two "deliberately break the server
and confirm the tool notices" passes — live against a real server rather than assuming
the fix worked, and watched the two previously-silent checks correctly flip to
"caught it" this time. Everything came back clean. `CLAUDE_DOCS/DEVELOPMENT_PLAN.md`

   was closed with a BASELINE entry mirroring R-2's shape. **That was wrong, and it was
   caught and fixed the same day, before being reported as final.** A BASELINE entry only
   has two modes — "still admitted" (fine) or "now refused" (treated as a regression,
   `BASELINE DRIFT`) — and this timing signal is genuinely probabilistic (it sits at this
   host's noise floor, so the sign is only *sometimes* stable). Baselining it did not
   remove the intermittent failure; it inverted which outcome counted as one, watched live
   on the very next CI run (`gate-instruments` run 33403084092 and `broken-control-check`
   run 33403084018, both against the same commit). **Fixed properly**: the check is now a
   `note()` — an observation, not a pass/fail gate — matching this probe's own long-standing
   comment ("Keep it, and do not treat it as the measurement"). The real, magnitude-bounded
   enforcement of §4.13's accepted bound is `authorization_timing_test.dart`, in the
   ordinary server suite on every commit; this HTTP-level probe was never that enforcement
   and should not have been made to act like it.

   validator before you know what a refusal costs.* Two things added on top of your
   write-up. **The rule must be an allowlist, not a longer denylist** — the previous list
   was written deliberately three days ago by somebody thinking about exactly this attack
   and still missed two characters, which is the argument made for us. And **the fix may

   baseline to make the flake go away. **§6's criterion 4 now carries an explicit verdict

   criterion with an unwritten precondition is one that will be met on paper on the day it
   matters.
4. **Michael answered, and he chose both options rather than one — which is right, because
   they solve different problems.** **Freeze the project name onto the request at the
   moment it is made, and expire decided requests** (his words: *"we wouldn't want that on
   their screen forever"*). Expiry alone still leaks renames for the whole retention
   window; freezing alone leaves a rejection on somebody's phone permanently. **Both are in
   task 11.79.** The freeze is the pattern that design already uses one column over — the
   requester's email is copied onto the row at request time — so this applies an existing
   decision rather than inventing one. **Window: 30 days unless he says otherwise**, long
   enough that somebody three weeks out of signal still gets their answer. And one detail
   that decides whether it reads as tidy or broken: **when the row expires the card is
   simply absent, not an empty state that looks like a failure.**
5. **Corrected, and the note is kept rather than deleted** — a Phase 11 finding filed under
   Phase 12's heading is worth a record of the near-miss, not a silent tidy-up. **Catching a
   filing error in somebody else's Discovered Scope is not something a task is asked to
   do**, and it is the kind of thing that goes unnoticed for months.
6. **Taken, and it is the more useful half of the estimate story.** The plan already records

### Task 11.83 — 2026-08-31 — commit `9a4d974` — Done

**What changed, in one sentence.** When a project owner approves somebody's request to
join, that person's phone now downloads the project by itself and says so on screen —
before, the approval landed on the server and nothing on their device turned it into a
project they could see.

**For the planning session**

1. **Task 11.83's spec did not anticipate a server change, and one was unavoidable —
   please check the disclosure argument.** `GET /projects/join-requests/mine` returned
   the decision and the project's *name*. A device cannot download a project it cannot
   name, and matching by name would have been a guess. It now returns `project_id`
   **on an approved request and on nothing else.** The argument that this discloses
   nothing new: an approved requester is already a member, and `GET /projects/mine`
   hands them the same id — so anybody the owner has not admitted still learns no
   project identifier. Two integration tests in
   `server/test/integration/membership_and_joining_test.dart` pin both halves
   (approved carries it, pending and rejected do not). **The rate limits were not
   touched**, as instructed.
2. **Ask task 11.85 to re-read inventory entry 29 against this change.** Entry 29 in
   `SECURITY_SCOPE_AND_EXIT.md` says a decided request must disclose "the decision and
   nothing else about the project". That wording is now literally false for an
   approval, deliberately and with the argument above — but **I did not edit that file,
   because the "Resolved"/verdict half of the scope document is the planning session's**
   and 11.85 is the round that attacks entry 29. Somebody has to update the wording or
   record why it stands.
3. **Two decisions I made that the spec left open. Both are one condition to reverse
   if you disagree.**
   - **The automatic check is gated on a durable "this device has join business" flag**
     (`SyncStateStore.joinWorkPending`). Without it every device asked the server on
     every foreground — including one whose owner had chosen "Only when I ask", which
     task 11.59's own suite caught immediately. A device that has never asked to join
     anything now reaches no server at all and costs one `SharedPreferences` read.
   - **The sync-frequency setting does *not* suppress the poll.** Somebody who has just
     tapped "Ask to join" is asking, and the join card tells them what will happen. The
     "Only when I ask" copy is scoped to syncing records ("Your records stay on this
     device until you tap Sync now"), so I read it as not covering this. **If you want
     the setting to cover it too, say so** — it is one condition in
     `JoinRequestWatcher._check`.
4. **A consequence worth a decision, not a defect.** A fresh install signing in as
   somebody with several historical approvals will auto-download **all** of those
   projects, bounded by the server's 200-request window. Every one is a project that
   person is a member of, so nothing wrong happens — but it could be a lot of cellular
   data on a phone. **Every bound I could think of (a recency window on the decision)
   needed a comparison between the server's clock and the device's**, which this task
   explicitly told me not to guess at, so I built no bound and am reporting it instead.
   If you want one, it needs a task.
5. **`myJoinRequestsProvider` is gone**, replaced by `JoinRequestWatcher` as the single

   (it is there, incomplete, and the rest arrives next time that project syncs), or
   *"the download hasn't started"* (it is not in your list yet, and it retries each time
   you open the app with a connection). Either way **you are still a member** — the
   approval is not lost.

### Task 11.78 — 2026-08-30 — commit 6918a9e — Done

**What changed, in one sentence.** `docker compose up` now starts a container
that takes an encrypted backup every day on its own, and `docker compose ps`
names the age of the newest archive — so nobody can believe they have backups
when the newest one is from setup week.

**The one number a person sees:** `newest backup: 6h old` / `NEWEST BACKUP IS 34
DAYS OLD` / `NO BACKUP HAS EVER BEEN TAKEN`. Stale and absent are deliberately
different sentences, and there is a fourth — "this container cannot read the
backup directory" — because task 11.70's whole finding was a message naming the
wrong cause.

**For the planning session**

1. **Add a task for the audit-log purge — it has exactly the gap 11.78 just
   closed, and a second defect besides.** Written up in full in Phase 11's
   Discovered Scope. Two facts: nothing runs `AuditRetentionService.purge()`, so
   the retention windows the documentation promises (a year for sign-in events,
   180 days for sync traffic) describe an intention rather than what is on disk;
   **and the command the documentation gave — `dart run
   bin/purge_audit_logs.dart` "e.g. a daily cron inside the container" — cannot
   run in the shipped server container at all**, because that image contains a
   compiled server binary and no Dart SDK or source. It works only on a
   developer's laptop. The README now says both things; nothing is fixed.
   **11.78's shape is the template and it should be roughly a day**: compile the
   purge entrypoint into the server image, schedule it the way
   `backup-scheduler` is scheduled, and measure **the age of the oldest
   surviving row** rather than whether a timer exists. Not beta-blocking — an
   unrun backup loses data, an unrun purge keeps rows past their window, which
   is a liability that grows rather than a loss — but it should land before the
   database holds more than one project's people.
2. **Record the decision I made about who is meant to notice, or overrule it.**
   The operator, and nobody else. A project owner in the app is not told and has
   no way to find out: the diagnostics console is off by default and
   loopback-only, and the sync screen belongs to a project rather than to a
   server. **If the operator and the project owner are different human beings,
   the owner has no signal at all** and no part of this repository can give them
   one without a new authenticated server route and a disclosure decision about
   what one project's owner may learn about the server. Written into
   `server/README.md` in those words. If that is not acceptable for beta, it
   needs a task.
3. **The 48-hour staleness threshold is mine, with a reason, and Michael has the
   final say.** One missed daily run is a reboot; two consecutive misses is a
   schedule that has stopped, and 48h bounds what is at risk to two days of
   observations. It is one line in `.env`
   (`TRITRACK_BACKUP_MAX_AGE_HOURS`) and the argument is in `server/README.md`.

4. **Task 11.70's Discovered Scope item is closed** — it named this and it is
   done.

1. **Nothing is committed for you to push yet beyond this commit — but read item
   2 first, it is about your own machine.**

### Task 11.71 — 2026-08-30 — commit eeb5950 — Done

**For the planning session**

1. **The blind check is closed, and the answer was your second explanation, not your
   first.** The check was correctly written and looking in the right place. Round 8's
   five traversal addresses simply could not put a file anywhere it looks: on Linux
   `%2f` and `\` are ordinary filename characters so two of them never leave the
   directory, two more name subdirectories `FileEmailSender` does not create, and the
   only one aimed outside — `../../../../etc/…` — is refused by the **filesystem**,
   because the container runs as an unprivileged user. So the control was holding for a
   reason other than the documented one.
2. **The real defence is named and written down, and it is narrower than it looks.**
   The unprivileged container user keeps an escape out of `/etc`. It does nothing about
   `/tmp` or `/var/tmp` — the same user writes to both freely, measured — and
   `docker-compose.e2e.yml`'s `user:` falls back to `0:0`, so a stack brought up without
   `scripts/lib/host_user.sh` gets `/etc` back. **The sanitiser is load-bearing and is
   now measured to be:** with it deleted, an unauthenticated `../../../../tmp/…` address
   makes the server create a caller-named file in `/tmp`. That is in §15.3 M-9 so a
   later refactor cannot read the unprivileged user as cover for removing the sanitiser.
3. **The gate's record is corrected in three places, and one of them was a false
   sentence rather than an over-claim of degree.** `SECURITY_SCOPE_AND_EXIT.md` entry 20
   ended "watched to fail: with the sanitiser deleted, the escape appears and the probe
   goes red." That was written before the harness had ever been run on a machine that
   could run it, and its first real run flipped seven of eight, not eight of eight. Entry
   20, its cost table row, and the security model's §21.1 and §21.2 now say what
   happened. **Entries 14 and 15 are unaffected** — their evidence is different probes,
   every one of which was watched flipping — and entry 20 is `Accepted`, so **no
   `Hardened` verdict is overturned.** Nothing needs re-running.
4. **One thing worth generalising, if you want a task for it: this class is "the attack
   corpus cannot reach the check", and it is not the same as a broken check.** Every
   control inside the instrument was firing correctly; the thing that was wrong was
   upstream of all of them, and only an outside harness that deletes the control could
   see it. Four of round 8's five addresses were, on Linux, decoration. **Other
   instruments in `scripts/` that end in a comprehensive search — a `find`, a grep of a
   whole log, a scan of a whole table — may have the same shape**, and I have not
   swept for it. If you think that sweep is worth a task, it is yours to schedule; I did
   not add one to Discovered Scope because it is a new piece of work rather than a
   follow-up to this one.

**For Michael**

1. **Nothing to run and nothing to decide.** Committed as `eeb5950`; push when you next
   push. The change is to two test scripts and three documents — no app or server code.
2. **The risk you were carrying is gone, and it was smaller than it looked.** The check
   that could not fail was the one asking "did a sign-in file escape onto the server's
   filesystem". It was reporting "no" for two rounds without being able to say anything
   else. It now genuinely says no, and it has been watched saying yes against a
   deliberately broken build.

---

### Task 11.72 — 2026-08-30 — commits `04a4903`, `9e6b72c`, `27c23ab`, `082fad8` — Done

Mostly fixed rather than accepted; the last few microseconds accepted in writing. The
task said to establish what cost the extra time before choosing, and that changed the
answer twice — once from the attribution, and once from the GitHub runner refusing the
first version of my answer.

**For the planning session**

1. **Record that the finding was larger than the brief described — that is what made
   fixing it the right option rather than accepting it.** The refusal was not leaking one
   bit. `ProjectAuthorizer.resolve` read **every membership row of the project**, so the
   time it took grew with the number of people on it: about 7 microseconds slower than a
   fictional id at one member, 17 at three, 71 at twenty, 213 at fifty, sign unanimous
   from three members up. **What that costs a person:** somebody with no access to a
   project — a removed collaborator, or anyone holding an id from a share payload — could
   read off roughly how big the team on it is, not merely that the id is real. The bar
   reading in the plan was applied to "confirms an id you already hold," and team size was
   not on the table when that was written. It is closed now either way, but the analysis
   should not stand as it is.

2. **The residual is accepted rather than closed, and the acceptance needs your review
   because I made it on Michael's behalf.** Both differences are down by a factor of forty
   to a hundred, and **neither is zero**: on the runner, **+6.0 microseconds** between a
   real project and a fictional id, **+4.0** between a fifty-member project and a
   one-member one, against a measured per-id noise floor of **4 microseconds on the same
   run** — so the residuals sit *on* the floor rather than above it. The reason they
   cannot go to zero: an index probe that finds a row does a heap fetch and one that finds
   nothing does not. Only padding removes that, and padding is rejected in writing
   (§4.13): the floor must exceed the slowest real project, it grows as teams grow, and
   `/sync/pull` has no per-user rate limit, so a padded refusal is a resource an attacker
   can hold. **I registered the acceptance with a reason, a date and a reopen condition
   that is a check rather than a promise** — each pair bounded at 25 microseconds, or four
   times the run's own floor if that is larger — and marked it subject to Michael's
   review, because the decision was his.

3. **The brief's "it shows on two different routes" is not what was measured, and I have
   corrected it in the security model.** The two probes that found it are independently
   written, which rules out one instrument being wrong — but they both call
   `POST /sync/pull`, so nothing ruled out one *handler* being wrong. The conclusion
   happened to be right: the function is called by the project-detail route and all three
   sync routes, so the difference was on four routes and the narrowing covers all four.

4. **The most useful thing this task produced is a rule about instruments, not about
   timing.** My first instrument asserted "no stable sign" on both pairs — written and
   verified on a Mac — and the runner refused it by reporting the *null pair* (two ids
   that both name nothing, whose true difference is exactly zero) unanimous at 4.1
   microseconds. **A sign test cannot say anything below its own machine's per-id offset,
   and I had claimed it could.** That is the mistake this task exists to correct, made by
   the task, one commit after writing it up. The general form worth carrying: **a control
   whose only job is to pass is not doing a job — the null pair's real work was to publish
   the floor, and once it did, the assertions had to change shape.**

5. **Two items that are not mine, and the first needs a task number.** The offline suite
   is red on the runner on `position_estimation_screen_test.dart` for two consecutive
   runs, and was red on `map_screen_test.dart` a run earlier — **and the commit it started
   on changed four documentation files and no client code at all**, so nothing introduced
   it. The log names the cause 59 times: `MissingPluginException` on `path_provider`'s
   `getApplicationSupportDirectory`, so something running in the background during a
   widget test reaches for a real device folder and there is no device. **And this is not
   a runner problem: I ran that file on the Mac and the same exceptions appear there while
   the test still passes.** So the exceptions are unconditional, and what is intermittent
   is only whether they land inside a test body, where the framework counts them, or after
   it, where nobody looks. That makes it cheaper to fix than a race and more urgent than a
   flake. **Task 11.69 fixed one race in the map screen and said it could not prove there
   was only one; this is the second.** Fix it as the class: if a plugin channel can be reached from a widget test,
   every screen test is a coin flip. Written up in Phase 11's Discovered Scope with what
   the task would be.

6. **The class sweep is done and found nothing else** — recorded in Discovered Scope and
   in §4.13. Asking for a magic link is clean, and better designed than what I fixed: it
   runs the same three statements whether or not the address has an account, because it
   never consults `auth_accounts` at all, so the one unauthenticated route where
   enumeration would really matter does not have this shape. **Said as a limit: that sweep
   is a reading of the code, not a measurement of it.** Only `ProjectAuthorizer.resolve`
   has an instrument.

**For Michael**

1. **Nothing to push — I committed and pushed four times and ran the workflows on GitHub,

3. **A decision was coming to you and it has mostly gone away, but a small piece is still

All four workflows' checks now pass on this machine. Two root causes, both

   `backup_restore_drill` and `verify_h6_archive_forgery` never touch a magic link;
   they failed because the backup container runs as its own `postgres` user (uid 70)
   and on Linux cannot create a file in the host directory the drill mounts, nor read
   the mode-600 signing key mounted out of it. The instruction to check the
   per-instrument logs first is what found it.

2. **Add a task for the backup ownership problem in the shipped deployment — this is
   the important one.** The same mismatch is live in what `server/README.md` tells a
   real operator to do. On a Linux server, the `backups/` directory they create and
   the mode-600 signing key they generate are both unusable by the container, and
   `backup.sh` reports `pg_dump | age pipeline failed; no archive written` — which
   names the wrong cause. **A person following the documented procedure ends up
   believing they have encrypted backups when no archive was ever written.** Task
   11.69 fixed the two drill scripts so the instruments run on Linux, and wrote the
   trap plus a `chown` workaround into `server/README.md`, **but the real fix is a
   §4.9 custody decision and needs your call between three shapes**: (a) the compose
   file declares a `user:` for the `backup` service, (b) the documented procedure
   gains a `chown` step, (c) the image stops running as `postgres`. They differ in
   who can read the signing key on a shared machine. Full write-up is in Phase 11's
   Discovered Scope. **Second cost, worth stating plainly: the drill passing is no
   longer evidence that a real deployment's backup can write its archive.**

3. **Decide what happens to a failing gate instrument's log in CI.**
   `gate_smoke_test.sh` keeps each instrument's full output in a `mktemp` directory
   on the runner and prints only `tail -n 5`. That directory dies with the runner, so
   the two backup failures above had to be diagnosed by reading scripts and reasoning
   about uid semantics rather than by reading what happened. **The obvious fix is
   blocked by a real constraint:** those logs can contain live session tokens, and
   §4.7's never-log rule names the CI artifact specifically. So this is a decision,
   not a chore — a redacted upload, or the five-line tail plus a `workflow_dispatch`
   re-run as the accepted answer. Either is defensible. Also in Discovered Scope.

   differently.** The brief offered excluding `server/` as defensible *if* the Server
   suite's own analyze covers what the root one would have. **It does not — nothing

   against growing an `exclude:` without someone writing down what coverage was
   given up.

   measuring a repository whose committed state did not match the machine they were

   say **two** Open entries rather than one.

   rather than mine — I gave it to task 11.49.** If a membership row carries a `role`
   word this build does not recognise, the person is left with an *open* stint, no
   access, and no disclosure: they still see "the server is refusing access". Handing
   back an open row would tell their device it is still a member of a project the
   server refuses, which is a worse answer than the one they get now. It needs a

   reachable today. It is in Phase 11's Discovered Scope naming task 11.49, and in
   Security Model §4.27.

   knowing about because two gates walked past it.** Asking the server about a project
   id that names nothing cost it one database query; asking about a real project that
   is somebody else's cost two. Those are the two answers §4.13 requires to be
   indistinguishable "from outside", and the amount of work done is visible from
   outside too. **I did not measure it** — over a network the difference is very
   likely below the noise — but task 11.60 was about to add a third query to that same
   path, so it is closed rather than built on. It is in Phase 11's Discovered Scope as
   found-and-closed.

4. **Task 11.60's own spec assumed a screen change and the work turned out to be
   mostly plumbing, which is worth carrying into how similar tasks are scoped.** The
   server change was about forty lines. What actually took the work was that the news
   had nowhere to travel: a device with records waiting had its push refused first,
   which threw before the pull that carries the answer could run; and the page that
   carries it does not move the sync cursor, which the client would then have tried to
   acknowledge — a write, still correctly refused, which would have discarded the page
   it had just saved. Both are now fixed and both are in `sync_engine.dart` with the
   reasoning next to them.

5. **Nothing needs re-scoping and no task needs adding.** Item 2 of the original
   11.60 had already moved to 11.62 before I started, and I did not touch ownership,

### Task 11.59 — 2026-08-29 — commit 88e7316 — Done
**For the planning session**
1. **Add a small task: `SyncSchedule.resumed()` has no caller anywhere in the app,
   and it is the second method in that file with that problem** — the first was
   `syncIfDue`, which is what task 11.59 existed to fix. It exists so that somebody
   who has just signed in again syncs immediately instead of waiting out the
   interval. **This task made it slightly more visible:** the time of the last sync
   attempt is now saved to disk, so a person who signs out and back in within their
   chosen interval now waits out the rest of it, where before any rebuild forgot the
   time and the next attempt went straight through. Nothing is lost, the bar does not
   lie about it, and "Sync now" is on the same screen — which is why I left it rather
   than widening this task. The fix is either to clear the saved attempt time when a
   session is established, or to delete the method. Written up in Phase 11's
   Discovered Scope.
2. **Note a behaviour change in the plan where it matters to a later task: the
   frequency setting is now a ceiling on how often the app reaches out.** The
   failure backoff used to start at one minute, which was free when fifteen minutes
   was the only cadence; under the new "Hourly" choice it would have meant an attempt
   every minute for as long as a server stayed unreachable. So the wait after a
   failure is now the longer of the backoff curve and the chosen interval. **The
   visible consequence for the default:** a transient failure is now retried after
   fifteen minutes rather than after one. I judged that the right trade — a setting
   that says "every 15 minutes" must not attempt more often than that — but it is a
   change to task 10.8's curve and somebody should know it was deliberate.
3. **Nothing else to schedule from this task.** The two remaining items below are
   Michael's, not the planning session's.

### Task 11.57 follow-up — 2026-08-29 — commit fc21a32 — Michael answered the automatic-sync question

**This is the answer to item 4 of the entry below**, which said the decision was
his. He gave it on 2026-08-29: **yes, the app should sync automatically, and the
sync screen should let the user change the sync frequency.** Nothing has been
implemented for it — this entry is the request for a task.

**For the planning session**

1. **Ask for a task: wire up automatic sync, and add a frequency control to the
   sync status screen.** Michael's decision, quoted above. Most of the machinery
   already exists and none of it is called: `SyncSchedule` (task 10.8) has an
   on/off setting defaulting to **on**, a fifteen-minute minimum interval,
   exponential backoff from one minute to a two-hour ceiling, and a terminal stop
   for a revoked session or a version mismatch. What is missing is the call site —
   `syncIfDue()` from the foreground hook in `app.dart`, beside the stuck-departure
   recovery task 11.57 put there — and the setting UI.

2. **The frequency control needs to be labelled for what the app actually does,
   and this is the part worth getting right rather than the interval values.**
   Task 10.8 decided deliberately, with reasons, that **there is no background
   sync**: iOS runs background work when it feels like it, which on a phone that
   spends the day in a pack is close to never, and registering for it costs
   battery on every wake. So "frequency" here does not mean *how often the app
   syncs*. It means *how long after the last attempt a foreground counts as due*.
   **If the app is closed all day, nothing syncs at any setting.** A control
   reading "Sync every 15 minutes" would therefore describe a mechanism the code
   does not have — which is the defect class tasks 11.54 and 11.57 both existed to
   close, arriving by a new door. Suggested shape, for the planning session to
   accept or replace:

   > **Sync while TriTrack is open**
   > Every time I open it · **Every 15 minutes (recommended)** · Hourly · Only
   > when I ask
   >
   > *TriTrack syncs while the app is open. It does not sync in the background.*

   A short list of named choices rather than a minutes field: a free number
   invites "1", which spends battery and data for nothing, and "1440", which is
   indistinguishable from off but does not say so.

3. **"Only when I ask" must be visible on the sync bar, and that is an acceptance
   line rather than a nicety.** Turning automatic sync off is a legitimate choice —
   satellite billing is the case task 10.8 named — but a device that is quietly not
   syncing, showing a bar that says "3 records waiting to sync", is telling
   somebody it is about to do something it will never do. This phase has spent
   three tasks removing exactly that silence from the sync surface; a new setting
   must not put it back. The bar should say sync is off, in those words.

4. **Two things that already hold and should become acceptance lines so they
   cannot regress.** (a) **Manual "Sync now" ignores the setting entirely** — this
   is already true (`SyncController.syncNow` bypasses the schedule) and is the
   whole point of the trailhead case task 10.8 was designed around. (b) The
   fifteen-minute floor exists so that foregrounding the app constantly — which
   field use does, between the map and the record screen — does not mean a round
   trip each time; an "every time I open it" option removes that floor and should
   be offered knowing so.

5. **Stated as uncertainty, because it is:** automatic sync is **not Wi-Fi-only**
   and can spend cellular data. `SyncSchedule`'s own header says so and says the
   remedy is to turn automatic sync off; a real "unmetered connections only"
   setting needs interface detection and was filed as follow-up scope. If the user
   is now being given a frequency control, that sentence belongs on the same
   screen as it. **I have not measured the battery or data cost of a fifteen-minute
   foreground cadence on real hardware** — the numbers above are task 10.8's
   reasoning, not a measurement, and the task should say whether it wants one.

**For Michael**

1. **Nothing to do — this is recorded and waiting on the planning session.** No
   code changed for it; the app still syncs only when you ask.
2. **One thing to know before you see the setting, because it will look like a
   bug otherwise:** whatever frequency you pick, TriTrack only syncs **while the
   app is open**. That was a deliberate decision (task 10.8) — background sync on
   iOS is unreliable enough that registering for it costs battery without
   delivering much. If that is not what you want, say so and it becomes a separate
   and considerably larger task.

### Task 11.57 — 2026-08-29 — commit fc21a32 — Done

**What changed, in one sentence.** A device could be a member of a project on the
server, be holding a hidden copy of it, and be shown nothing at all — no project,
no sync bar, no warning, and no way back; it now gets the project offered under
"Join a project", which restores the copy already on the device rather than
fetching a new one over the top of it.

**For the planning session**

1. **Ask for a task, and it is the biggest thing this task found: nothing in the
   app ever starts a sync on its own.** `SyncController.syncIfDue` exists,
   documents itself as the opportunistic/foreground attempt, and has **no caller
   anywhere in `lib/`**. Syncing happens only when somebody opens the Sync Status
   screen, retries a refused record, or changes a membership. A person recording
   bearings all day and never opening that screen has nothing on the server, and
   the bar says *"N records waiting to sync"*, which reads as "about to" and means
   "not until you ask". Written up in Phase 11's Discovered Scope. **It needs a
   decision from Michael before it needs code** — automatic sync on foreground is
   a battery-and-data choice.
2. **Ask for a task: somebody an owner removed cannot delete their local copy
   without first pressing "Leave".** Measured, and in the matrix. The
   departed-member exemption checks the *local* membership rows, and a removed
   person's device never learns it was removed — the pull that would tell them is
   the request being refused. A route out exists (press Leave, then Delete) and
   nothing tells anybody to use it. The fix is a decision, not an obvious edit:
   either the app lets somebody delete a copy of a project it cannot reach, or the
   server hands a removed member their own closed row, which is a disclosure
   question. In Discovered Scope.
3. **Low, but it will bite the day task 11.1 gets a button:** an ownership
   transfer (`grantOwner` inserting a membership row for somebody else) is refused
   by the server unconditionally and correctly withheld by the client, so it fails
   silently at both ends. There is no UI caller today. An invitation issued at
   `owner` role does work end to end — the matrix walks it — so that may be the
   whole answer. In Discovered Scope.
4. **Two corrections to the record, both of which were reasonable readings that
   measurement overturned.** (a) Item 3's leading hypothesis — that a departure is
   refused because a column is not byte-identical to the server's stored row — is
   **wrong**. Read against the real server: a departure is accepted on the first
   attempt. What is true is that the round always throws *afterwards*, because the
   pull that follows the accepted departure is refused — the person is no longer a
   member. That is the "leaving reports a sync failure" symptom, and it is
   expected. (b) The Discovered Scope entry that opens with "NEEDS A TASK NUMBER"
   for the membership cycle now has one — this task — and can be retired.
5. **A property this project relies on was written too widely and is now
   corrected.** `offer_rules.dart` said *"nothing withheld here could ever have
   been accepted"*. That is true of a row the server has never seen and was being
   applied to updates as well, where it is false — which is how an owner's removal
   of a member was withheld from every push for as long as the feature has
   existed. Worth knowing because it is this project's recurring shape: a control
   that works for a reason other than the documented one.

**For Michael**

1. **Nothing to do to unstick your phone beyond installing this build.** Open
   More → Projects → the cloud icon ("Join a project"). The project you left and
   deleted will be listed, marked *"Already on this device but not syncing"*, with
   a **Restore** button instead of Join. Restoring puts back everything that was
   on the phone — it does not download a fresh empty copy over it.
2. **Before you restore it, nothing is at risk either way** — I checked what the
   fix does to records already on the device, and the answer is nothing: it clears
   the hidden-delete mark and resumes syncing, then pushes whatever had been
   waiting. Whether anything actually *was* waiting on your phone I cannot tell
   from here; the app will tell you after the restore, on the sync bar.
3. **Please try the two things this task could not:** (a) have the Mac remove you
   from a project and check that the Mac's member list shows your stint ended
   *after it next syncs* — that direction never worked before today and now does
   in the lab, but it has never run on your hardware; (b) leave a project with the
   phone in airplane mode, delete it, then turn the network back on and reopen the
   app — the departure should go out by itself within a few seconds of the app
   coming to the foreground.
4. **One decision only you can make: should the app sync by itself?** Today it
   syncs when you open the Sync Status screen and at almost no other time. That is
   very likely not what you want for a field device, but turning on automatic sync
   spends battery and cellular data, so I have not changed it. Tell the planning
   session what you want and it becomes a task.
5. **A risk you are now carrying, and it is small but real.** If somebody is
   removed from a project by an owner, their device shows an amber *"the server is
   refusing access"* and they cannot delete their copy until they press "Leave"
   first. Nothing is lost and nothing leaks — their old copy just sits there. If a
   beta tester hits it, tell them to press Leave and then Delete.
6. **The "More" header question is closed and you do not owe a photograph.** All
   22 screen headers share one 18px style and no screen overrides it, so "More"
   was never larger than any other. The sync bar sat directly above the title, and
   the two read as one tall block; when the bar went away — because the phone had
